skills: 3.1.3: Choosing the deployment strategy.
questions.question: Your team has trained a monthly customer segmentation model. The downstream marketing pipeline reads scored records from Cloud Storage every morning to generate targeted email campaigns for the day. Latency of individual predictions does not matter, but you want to minimize compute cost. What should you do?
questions.tip: When predictions are consumed once per day from a file in Cloud Storage, the right serving path is the one that does not pay for an idle endpoint between runs.

choices.text: Batch prediction job
choices.explanation: The marketing pipeline reads from Cloud Storage each morning, so predictions can be generated overnight in a batch job. There is no idle compute cost between runs.

choices.text: Online endpoint with synchronous REST calls
choices.explanation: An always-on online endpoint incurs continuous instance costs even when not in use, which is unnecessary when predictions are only consumed once per day.

choices.text: Canary deployment with traffic splitting
choices.explanation: Canary deployment is a release strategy for gradually shifting traffic to a new model version; it does not address whether to use batch or online serving.

choices.text: Shadow deployment
choices.explanation: Shadow deployment runs a new model in parallel with the production model for comparison purposes; it is not a serving pattern for delivering daily marketing predictions.

questions.explanation:
Batch prediction jobs process a fixed dataset of inputs, write results to Cloud Storage, and then shut down, making them the most cost-efficient option when latency is not critical and results are consumed on a schedule.

**Why it works:** The marketing pipeline reads from Cloud Storage each morning, so predictions can be generated overnight in a batch job. There is no idle compute cost between runs.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Online endpoint: Keeps compute running 24/7 even though predictions are only needed once per day, wasting budget.
- Canary deployment: A release management technique, not a choice between batch and online serving.
- Shadow deployment: Used to validate a new model against production traffic, not to produce daily segmentation results.

skills: 3.1.3: Choosing the deployment strategy.
questions.question:
An ML team is deploying a new version of their production fraud detection model that serves 10,000 online requests per second. They need to minimize customer impact from any regression in the new model's performance. The team wants to validate real production traffic patterns before committing to a full rollout, and they must be able to instantly revert to the current model if metrics degrade.

Which deployment strategy BEST satisfies these requirements?
questions.tip: Think about which strategy allows the new model to receive a small, controlled percentage of live production traffic while preserving an instant fallback path.

choices.text: Canary deployment with traffic splitting on a Vertex AI endpoint
choices.explanation: Vertex AI endpoint traffic splitting lets the team set an exact percentage for the canary version. If latency or accuracy metrics degrade, the split is adjusted back to 0% for the new version within seconds.

choices.text: Blue-green deployment with immediate full traffic cutover
choices.explanation: Blue-green deployment switches 100% of traffic to the new version at once, which does not minimize customer impact during validation and makes rollback a deliberate re-switch rather than a traffic-percentage adjustment.

choices.text: Shadow deployment
choices.explanation: Shadow deployment sends copies of traffic to the new model but serves responses only from the existing model; it validates predictions in isolation but does not expose the new model to real consequence, so customer impact from a bad model is not observable.

choices.text: Batch prediction job
choices.explanation: Batch jobs process offline data and cannot serve real-time fraud detection requests at 10,000 requests per second.

questions.explanation:
Canary deployment routes a small percentage of live production traffic (e.g., 5%) to the new model version while the existing model continues to serve the rest, allowing real-world validation with limited blast radius and instant rollback by adjusting the traffic split.

**Why it works:** Vertex AI endpoint traffic splitting lets the team set an exact percentage for the canary version. If latency or accuracy metrics degrade, the split is adjusted back to 0% for the new version within seconds.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Blue-green with immediate cutover: Exposes all 10,000 RPS to the new model at once, creating maximum customer impact if the model regresses.
- Shadow deployment: The new model's outputs are not served to customers, so any regression has no business impact, but neither does it validate end-to-end production behavior.
- Batch prediction: Cannot fulfill real-time fraud detection needs.

skills: 3.1.3: Choosing the deployment strategy.
questions.question:
An ML platform team is defining deployment guidelines for two workloads. The first workload is a price optimization model that runs once per night to generate updated prices for 5 million products stored in BigQuery; results are read by an ETL pipeline the next morning. The second workload is a real-time recommendation model for a mobile app that must respond within 200 ms per user request. The team must select the correct deployment strategy for each workload.

Which two deployment strategies should the team recommend? (Choose 2)
questions.tip: Separate the workloads by whether the consumer needs an answer immediately or can wait for a scheduled run to complete.

choices.text: Batch prediction job writing results to BigQuery for the price optimization model
choices.explanation: Batch prediction jobs scale to process millions of rows efficiently and write to BigQuery at low cost. Online endpoints with autoscaling handle bursty real-time traffic within latency SLAs.

choices.text: Online endpoint with autoscaling for the recommendation model
choices.explanation: Batch prediction jobs scale to process millions of rows efficiently and write to BigQuery at low cost. Online endpoints with autoscaling handle bursty real-time traffic within latency SLAs.

choices.text: Online endpoint for the price optimization model
choices.explanation: An always-on online endpoint for a model that runs once per night wastes compute budget and provides no latency benefit over a batch job for this use case.

choices.text: Batch prediction job for the recommendation model
choices.explanation: Batch jobs cannot fulfill sub-200 ms per-request latency for real-time mobile app recommendations; they process fixed input sets and write outputs to storage.

choices.text: Shadow deployment for the recommendation model
choices.explanation: Shadow deployment is a release management strategy, not a primary serving pattern for production traffic.

questions.explanation:
The price optimization workload is a scheduled, high-volume, offline job where batch prediction is optimal. The recommendation workload requires low-latency, per-request serving where an autoscaling online endpoint is appropriate.

**Why it works:** Batch prediction jobs scale to process millions of rows efficiently and write to BigQuery at low cost. Online endpoints with autoscaling handle bursty real-time traffic within latency SLAs.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Online endpoint for price optimization: Costs more for 24/7 compute and offers no benefit when predictions are only consumed once per day.
- Batch job for recommendations: Latency is minutes to hours, far exceeding the 200 ms requirement.
- Shadow deployment for recommendations: A validation strategy, not a primary serving architecture.

skills: 3.1.3: Choosing the deployment strategy.
questions.question:
An ML team is rolling out a new production model using a staged release process designed to minimize risk. They start by validating behavior on live traffic without customer impact, then gradually expose real customers before completing a full cutover.

Order the following deployment stages from FIRST (least customer exposure) to LAST (full production cutover).
questions.tip: Think about which stage provides zero customer impact, which provides partial impact, and which represents full commitment to the new model.

choices.text: Shadow deployment: the new model receives mirrored traffic but responses are not served to customers
choices.explanation: Shadow deployment validates prediction quality and latency without any customer risk.

choices.text: Canary deployment: 5% of live production traffic is routed to the new model with real customer impact
choices.explanation: The 5% canary measures real-world impact at low blast radius.

choices.text: Canary deployment: traffic split increased to 50% after canary metrics are healthy
choices.explanation: The 50% canary confirms behavior at scale.

choices.text: Blue-green cutover: 100% of traffic switched to the new model and old model decommissioned
choices.explanation: The blue-green cutover completes the rollout once confidence is established.

questions.explanation:
A best-practice staged rollout moves from zero customer impact (shadow) to partial exposure (canary at low percentage) to majority exposure (canary at high percentage) before full cutover (blue-green switch).

**Why it works:** Shadow deployment validates prediction quality and latency without any customer risk. The 5% canary measures real-world impact at low blast radius. The 50% canary confirms behavior at scale. The blue-green cutover completes the rollout once confidence is established.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Starting with the blue-green cutover skips validation and maximizes risk.
- Skipping shadow deployment means latency and correctness issues are not caught before real customer exposure.
- Jumping from shadow directly to 50% canary skips the low-risk 5% validation step.

skills: 3.1.4: Applying modeling techniques given interpretability requirements.
questions.question:
A bank is building a credit approval model that must comply with fair lending regulations. Regulators require that for every declined application the bank can provide a ranked list of the specific input features that most influenced the decision. The data science team is evaluating which modeling technique to use.

Which approach BEST satisfies the regulatory interpretability requirement?
questions.tip: Think about which technique produces a per-prediction attribution score for every input feature, without requiring the model itself to be inherently simple.

choices.text: Vertex Explainable AI using Shapley values
choices.explanation: Shapley values have a solid game-theoretic foundation that satisfies the regulatory need for consistency and completeness. Vertex Explainable AI integrates directly with Vertex AI endpoints, applying SHAP or sampled Shapley attribution alongside each prediction.

choices.text: Deep Neural Network without any post-hoc explanation method
choices.explanation: A DNN without an explanation method produces only a prediction score; it cannot generate a ranked list of feature contributions for individual decisions.

choices.text: ARIMA time-series model
choices.explanation: ARIMA is a univariate forecasting model and cannot classify credit applications or produce per-feature attribution for individual loan decisions.

choices.text: k-means clustering
choices.explanation: k-means is an unsupervised clustering algorithm that assigns group membership; it does not produce the per-sample feature attribution required for declined-application explanations.

questions.explanation:
Vertex Explainable AI uses Shapley values to compute a contribution score for each feature on every individual prediction, allowing the bank to tell each declined applicant exactly which features drove the decision.

**Why it works:** Shapley values have a solid game-theoretic foundation that satisfies the regulatory need for consistency and completeness. Vertex Explainable AI integrates directly with Vertex AI endpoints, applying SHAP or sampled Shapley attribution alongside each prediction.

**Why the others don't work:**
- DNN without explanation: Produces a probability score only; regulators require feature-level reasons.
- ARIMA: A time-series forecasting model with no ability to classify or attribute features for a credit decision.
- k-means: An unsupervised method that clusters data points; it does not generate per-decision feature attributions.

skills: 3.1.4: Applying modeling techniques given interpretability requirements.
questions.question: Your insurance company has trained a gradient-boosted tree model to predict property claim amounts. Offline performance is good, but the business risk team requires that a claims adjuster be able to understand and challenge any prediction. The model took six months to develop and validate and cannot be replaced. You want to add an interpretability layer that works on the existing trained model. What should you do?
questions.tip: When the model is fixed and you need per-prediction feature attributions, look for a post-hoc model-agnostic technique.

choices.text: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) applied post-hoc to the trained model
choices.explanation: SHAP requires only the trained model's predict function and the input data, making it compatible with gradient boosted trees without modification. Each prediction comes with a signed attribution for every feature, enabling adjusters to challenge specific inputs.

choices.text: Retrain the model as a logistic regression
choices.explanation: Replacing the gradient boosted tree with logistic regression would destroy six months of development and likely degrade predictive accuracy; it is not a post-hoc technique.

choices.text: Apply ARIMA to the prediction outputs
choices.explanation: ARIMA is a time-series model and cannot interpret or explain the feature contributions behind an individual claim amount prediction.

choices.text: Add dropout layers to the existing gradient boosted tree
choices.explanation: Dropout is a regularization technique for neural networks and cannot be applied to tree-based models; it does not produce feature-level explanations.

questions.explanation:
SHAP is a model-agnostic, post-hoc explanation method that computes feature contribution scores for any trained model's individual predictions using Shapley values from cooperative game theory.

**Why it works:** SHAP requires only the trained model's predict function and the input data, making it compatible with gradient boosted trees without modification. Each prediction comes with a signed attribution for every feature, enabling adjusters to challenge specific inputs.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Logistic regression retraining: A model replacement strategy, not an interpretability layer, and it discards the existing validated model.
- ARIMA on outputs: ARIMA processes time-series numbers and cannot reverse-engineer feature attributions from a tree model's predictions.
- Dropout on trees: Dropout is a neural network concept inapplicable to decision tree ensembles.

skills: 3.1.4: Applying modeling techniques given interpretability requirements.
questions.question:
A healthcare organization is evaluating modeling techniques for a readmission risk prediction system. Clinical leadership requires that clinicians can understand and trust individual predictions, and the legal team requires that model decisions can be audited. The data science team is debating between two broad strategies: using an inherently interpretable model or applying a post-hoc explanation technique to a black-box model.

Which two approaches provide valid paths to satisfying the interpretability requirement? (Choose 2)
questions.tip: Think about which model types are transparent by design and which post-hoc technique produces locally faithful explanations that meet audit needs.

choices.text: Train a regularized logistic regression model and report the model coefficients as feature importance
choices.explanation: Logistic regression coefficients are transparent and auditable without additional tooling. Shapley values decompose any prediction into additive feature contributions with formal theoretical guarantees, satisfying both clinical understanding and legal auditability.

choices.text: Apply Vertex Explainable AI with Shapley values to a trained neural network model
choices.explanation: Logistic regression coefficients are transparent and auditable without additional tooling. Shapley values decompose any prediction into additive feature contributions with formal theoretical guarantees, satisfying both clinical understanding and legal auditability.

choices.text: Use a k-nearest neighbors model without any explanation layer
choices.explanation: k-NN can be inspected conceptually by examining neighbors, but it does not natively produce the per-feature attribution scores required for clinical and legal audit trails.

choices.text: Apply ARIMA to the tabular readmission features
choices.explanation: ARIMA is a univariate time-series forecasting model and cannot classify patients or attribute risk to individual clinical features.

choices.text: Train a deep neural network and report raw output logits as explanations
choices.explanation: Raw output logits represent the model's confidence scores, not feature attributions; they do not explain which inputs drove a prediction and do not satisfy audit requirements.

questions.explanation:
Logistic regression is inherently interpretable because its coefficients directly express the relationship between each feature and the outcome. Vertex Explainable AI with Shapley values provides locally faithful post-hoc explanations for any model, including neural networks.

**Why it works:** Logistic regression coefficients are transparent and auditable without additional tooling. Shapley values decompose any prediction into additive feature contributions with formal theoretical guarantees, satisfying both clinical understanding and legal auditability.

**Why the others don't work:**
- k-NN without explanation layer: Neighbor inspection is informal and does not produce quantitative feature attribution for each prediction.
- ARIMA: Cannot process multi-feature tabular patient data or produce classification outputs.
- Raw logits as explanations: Confidence scores are not feature attributions and cannot answer questions about which clinical variables drove a readmission prediction.

skills: 3.1.4: Applying modeling techniques given interpretability requirements.
questions.question:
A machine learning governance team is categorizing interpretability techniques. Each technique has a distinct scope (global vs. local), mechanism, and applicable model type. Understanding these distinctions helps practitioners choose the right tool for each compliance scenario.

Match each interpretability technique to its correct description.
questions.tip: Focus on whether each technique explains the model as a whole or a single prediction, and whether it requires access to model internals.

slots.label: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations)
slots.answer: A model-agnostic post-hoc technique that assigns each feature a signed contribution value for a single prediction using cooperative game theory.

slots.label: Linear model coefficients
slots.answer: An intrinsic global explanation in which each coefficient directly represents the feature's additive effect on the model output across all predictions.

slots.label: Surrogate model
slots.answer: An interpretable proxy model (e.g., a decision tree) trained to approximate a black-box model's behavior globally or locally, then used to explain predictions.

slots.label: Integrated Gradients (as used in Vertex Explainable AI)
slots.answer: A gradient-based attribution technique for differentiable models that measures how much each feature contributed relative to a defined baseline input.

choices.text: A model-agnostic post-hoc technique that assigns each feature a signed contribution value for a single prediction using cooperative game theory.
choices.explanation: SHAP is local and model-agnostic, using Shapley values.

choices.text: An intrinsic global explanation in which each coefficient directly represents the feature's additive effect on the model output across all predictions.
choices.explanation: Linear coefficients are global and intrinsic to the model.

choices.text: An interpretable proxy model (e.g., a decision tree) trained to approximate a black-box model's behavior globally or locally, then used to explain predictions.
choices.explanation: Surrogate models are post-hoc proxies that can be global or local.

choices.text: A gradient-based attribution technique for differentiable models that measures how much each feature contributed relative to a defined baseline input.
choices.explanation: Integrated Gradients are local and require gradient access, which Vertex Explainable AI uses for neural network models.

questions.explanation:
These four techniques cover the main axes of the interpretability landscape: scope (global vs. local), mechanism (intrinsic vs. post-hoc), and model compatibility (agnostic vs. gradient-based).

**Why it works:** SHAP is local and model-agnostic, using Shapley values. Linear coefficients are global and intrinsic to the model. Surrogate models are post-hoc proxies that can be global or local. Integrated Gradients are local and require gradient access, which Vertex Explainable AI uses for neural network models.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Swapping SHAP and Integrated Gradients ignores that IG requires differentiability while SHAP does not.
- Describing coefficients as post-hoc is incorrect because they are computed during training as part of the model itself.
- Describing a surrogate as intrinsic is incorrect because it is trained separately from the black-box model.

skills: 3.2.1: Organizing training data (e.g., tabular, text, speech, images, and videos) on Google Cloud (e.g., Cloud Storage and BigQuery).
questions.tip: Consider what data format and query pattern each service is optimized for.
questions.question:
A machine learning team is building an image classification model to detect defects in manufactured parts. The dataset consists of 500,000 JPEG images averaging 2 MB each, along with a CSV file containing metadata such as part ID, capture timestamp, and defect label. The team needs to store both the images and metadata on Google Cloud so they can be efficiently accessed during training.

Which storage configuration BEST organizes this training data?

choices.text: Store the JPEG images in Cloud Storage and load the metadata CSV into a BigQuery table.
choices.explanation: This split leverages each service's strengths. Training code reads image paths from BigQuery metadata rows, then streams the corresponding JPEG files from Cloud Storage using the GCS URI, which is the standard pattern for large-scale image training on Google Cloud.

choices.text: Store both the JPEG images and the metadata CSV in BigQuery as BYTES columns.
choices.explanation: Storing images in BigQuery as BYTES columns is technically possible but prohibitively expensive, bypasses BigQuery's query strengths, and causes large scan costs for every training epoch.

choices.text: Store the JPEG images in Cloud Bigtable and the metadata CSV in Cloud Storage.
choices.explanation: Cloud Bigtable is a NoSQL wide-column store suited for low-latency operational workloads, not batch ML training pipelines accessing unstructured image data.

choices.text: Store the JPEG images and metadata CSV together in a Cloud Filestore NFS share.
choices.explanation: Cloud Filestore is an NFS solution for applications needing a shared POSIX filesystem, not optimized for the high-throughput parallel reads typical in distributed ML training.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Storage is designed for unstructured binary objects like images, audio, and video, providing cheap, durable, scalable object storage accessible from training jobs. BigQuery is optimized for structured tabular data and supports fast SQL queries over metadata.

**Why it works:** This split leverages each service's strengths. Training code reads image paths from BigQuery metadata rows, then streams the corresponding JPEG files from Cloud Storage using the GCS URI, which is the standard pattern for large-scale image training on Google Cloud.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Storing images in BigQuery as BYTES columns is technically possible but prohibitively expensive, bypasses BigQuery's query strengths, and causes large scan costs for every training epoch.
- Cloud Bigtable is a NoSQL wide-column store suited for low-latency operational workloads, not batch ML training pipelines accessing unstructured image data.
- Cloud Filestore is an NFS solution for applications needing a shared POSIX filesystem, not optimized for the high-throughput parallel reads typical in distributed ML training.

skills: 3.2.1: Organizing training data (e.g., tabular, text, speech, images, and videos) on Google Cloud (e.g., Cloud Storage and BigQuery).
questions.tip: Think about what file format minimizes storage and maximizes read throughput for columnar ML training workloads.
questions.question:
A data science team is preparing a dataset of 50 million structured customer records stored in BigQuery for use in training a gradient-boosted tree model. Each record contains 120 numeric and categorical features. They want to export the data from BigQuery into a format that is efficient for training on Vertex AI custom training jobs and minimizes storage costs in Cloud Storage.

Which export format and storage approach should they use?

choices.text: Export the BigQuery table to Cloud Storage as gzip-compressed CSV files.
choices.explanation: Gzip-compressed CSV is row-oriented and requires decompressing the entire file before parsing, which is slow and memory-intensive for datasets with 120 columns.

choices.text: Export the BigQuery table to Cloud Storage as Parquet files.
choices.explanation: Parquet's columnar layout means training code can read only the feature columns it needs without scanning the full row, and built-in Snappy or GZIP compression significantly reduces storage size and network I/O. TensorFlow, PyTorch, and XGBoost all have first-class Parquet readers.

choices.text: Export the BigQuery table to Cloud Storage as Avro files without compression.
choices.explanation: Avro without compression is a row-based format well-suited for schema evolution and streaming, but it lacks the columnar read efficiency of Parquet and has no size benefit without compression.

choices.text: Leave the data in BigQuery and read directly using the BigQuery Storage Read API during every training epoch.
choices.explanation: Reading directly from BigQuery via the Storage Read API during every training epoch introduces per-epoch latency and cost from BigQuery slot consumption; pre-exporting to Cloud Storage is the standard cost-efficient pattern.

questions.explanation:
Parquet is a columnar binary format that combines efficient compression with fast column-selective reads, making it ideal for ML training over wide structured datasets stored in Cloud Storage.

**Why it works:** Parquet's columnar layout means training code can read only the feature columns it needs without scanning the full row, and built-in Snappy or GZIP compression significantly reduces storage size and network I/O. TensorFlow, PyTorch, and XGBoost all have first-class Parquet readers.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Gzip-compressed CSV is row-oriented and requires decompressing the entire file before parsing, which is slow and memory-intensive for datasets with 120 columns.
- Avro without compression is a row-based format well-suited for schema evolution and streaming, but it lacks the columnar read efficiency of Parquet and has no size benefit without compression.
- Reading directly from BigQuery via the Storage Read API during every training epoch introduces per-epoch latency and cost from BigQuery slot consumption; pre-exporting to Cloud Storage is the standard cost-efficient pattern.

skills: 3.2.1: Organizing training data (e.g., tabular, text, speech, images, and videos) on Google Cloud (e.g., Cloud Storage and BigQuery).

Which TWO properties of Cloud Storage are MOST relevant for this decision?

choices.text: Cloud Storage supports strong consistency for object reads after writes, ensuring training jobs always read the latest version of each audio file.
choices.explanation: Strong consistency ensures training code reading newly uploaded WAV files always retrieves the correct object rather than a stale version. Lifecycle management lets teams automatically archive older training data to Nearline or Coldline storage, reducing long-term costs without manual intervention.

choices.text: Cloud Storage provides object lifecycle management policies that can automatically transition cold training data to lower-cost storage classes.
choices.explanation: Strong consistency ensures training code reading newly uploaded WAV files always retrieves the correct object rather than a stale version. Lifecycle management lets teams automatically archive older training data to Nearline or Coldline storage, reducing long-term costs without manual intervention.

choices.text: Cloud Storage natively indexes audio and video content for full-text search, enabling metadata queries across recordings.

choices.text: Cloud Storage enforces column-level encryption and row-level access controls identical to BigQuery.

Cloud Storage is the canonical home for unstructured binary objects like audio and video in Google Cloud ML pipelines, and two of its key properties are strong read-after-write consistency and lifecycle management for cost control.

**Why it works:** Strong consistency ensures training code reading newly uploaded WAV files always retrieves the correct object rather than a stale version. **Why the others don't work:**

- Cloud Storage uses object-level and bucket-level IAM and CMEK encryption, not BigQuery-style column-level or row-level access controls.

skills: 3.2.1: Organizing training data (e.g., tabular, text, speech, images, and videos) on Google Cloud (e.g., Cloud Storage and BigQuery).
questions.question:
The training team stores 2 TB of labelled image data as TFRecord files in Cloud Storage, sharded into 500 files. A team member writes the following tf.data pipeline.

```python
import tensorflow as tf

file_pattern = 'gs://ml-bucket/train/images-*.tfrecord'
files = tf.data.Dataset.list_files(file_pattern, shuffle=True)

dataset = files.flat_map(tf.data.TFRecordDataset)
dataset = dataset.map(parse_fn, num_parallel_calls=tf.data.AUTOTUNE)
dataset = dataset.batch(128).prefetch(tf.data.AUTOTUNE)
```

The GPU utilisation is consistently below 40% during training. What change would MOST improve GPU utilisation without changing the model or hardware?

choices.text: Replace flat_map with interleave and add cycle_length and num_parallel_calls=tf.data.AUTOTUNE to read multiple TFRecord shards concurrently and overlap I/O with training.
choices.explanation: interleave with cycle_length and num_parallel_calls reads from multiple shard files in parallel, hiding I/O latency. flat_map reads shards sequentially, which causes the GPU to stall waiting for data.

choices.text: Increase the batch size from 128 to 1024 so each training step processes more images, reducing the ratio of data-loading time to compute time.
choices.explanation: A larger batch size can help amortise per-step overhead but does not fix the root cause: sequential shard reading. Without parallel I/O, the GPU still stalls waiting for the next batch.

choices.text: Add dataset.cache() after the map step so all 2 TB of parsed images are stored in memory, eliminating repeated GCS reads on subsequent epochs.
choices.explanation: Caching 2 TB in memory is not feasible on standard training VMs. Even if memory were sufficient, cache() does not solve the low GPU utilisation during the first epoch, which is caused by sequential shard reads.

choices.text: Move the .shuffle() call to after .batch() so that entire batches are shuffled rather than individual files, reducing the time spent on file-level randomisation.
choices.explanation: Shuffling batches rather than individual samples reduces randomness quality and does not address the I/O bottleneck. The low GPU utilisation is caused by sequential file reads, not shuffle overhead.

questions.tip: Low GPU utilisation in a tf.data pipeline typically indicates a data-loading bottleneck - consider how many shard files are being read simultaneously.
questions.explanation:
Using `flat_map` reads TFRecord shards one at a time. Replacing it with `interleave(cycle_length=N, num_parallel_calls=tf.data.AUTOTUNE)` reads from N shards concurrently, overlapping GCS I/O with GPU computation and dramatically reducing data starvation.

**Why it works:** `interleave` with parallelism saturates the I/O pipeline, keeping the preprocessing and batching steps ahead of the GPU's consumption rate.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Larger batch: reduces per-step overhead but doesn't fix sequential shard reads.
- cache(): 2 TB cannot fit in RAM; does not help epoch 1.
- Batch-level shuffle: reduces data quality without addressing the I/O bottleneck.

skills: 3.2.2: Ingesting structured and unstructured data from various sources into training pipelines.
questions.tip: Think about which API is specifically designed for building efficient, scalable input pipelines in TensorFlow.
questions.question:
A machine learning engineer is building a TensorFlow training job on Vertex AI to train a text classification model. The training dataset consists of 10 million labeled text records stored as TFRecord files in a Cloud Storage bucket. The engineer wants to build an efficient input pipeline that prefetches data, shuffles examples, and batches them for training.

Which approach should the engineer use to ingest the data into the training pipeline?

choices.text: Use `tf.data.TFRecordDataset` with `.shuffle()`, `.batch()`, and `.prefetch()` transformations to stream data from Cloud Storage.
choices.explanation: `TFRecordDataset` reads files directly from GCS URIs without requiring a full local copy. Chaining `.shuffle()`, `.batch()`, and `.prefetch(tf.data.AUTOTUNE)` creates a pipelined input that keeps the GPU fed with preprocessed batches while the previous batch is being trained on, eliminating I/O bottlenecks.

choices.text: Download all TFRecord files to the training VM's local disk at startup using `gsutil cp` before beginning training.
choices.explanation: Downloading all files to local disk at startup adds significant startup latency, requires large boot disk capacity, and negates Cloud Storage's scalability benefits for multi-worker training.

choices.text: Load all TFRecord files into a Pandas DataFrame in memory and convert to a TensorFlow tensor at the start of each epoch.
choices.explanation: Loading all records into a Pandas DataFrame requires fitting the entire dataset in memory, which is infeasible for 10 million records, and the conversion overhead at each epoch is prohibitive.

choices.text: Use the BigQuery Storage Read API to stream TFRecord data directly into the training loop without any preprocessing.
choices.explanation: The BigQuery Storage Read API streams rows from BigQuery tables, not from TFRecord files in Cloud Storage; it cannot directly read the TFRecord format.

questions.explanation:
`tf.data.TFRecordDataset` is TensorFlow's native API for streaming structured binary data from Cloud Storage, and its pipeline transformations are designed to maximize GPU utilization by overlapping data loading with model computation.

**Why it works:** `TFRecordDataset` reads files directly from GCS URIs without requiring a full local copy. Chaining `.shuffle()`, `.batch()`, and `.prefetch(tf.data.AUTOTUNE)` creates a pipelined input that keeps the GPU fed with preprocessed batches while the previous batch is being trained on, eliminating I/O bottlenecks.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Downloading all files to local disk at startup adds significant startup latency, requires large boot disk capacity, and negates Cloud Storage's scalability benefits for multi-worker training.
- Loading all records into a Pandas DataFrame requires fitting the entire dataset in memory, which is infeasible for 10 million records, and the conversion overhead at each epoch is prohibitive.
- The BigQuery Storage Read API streams rows from BigQuery tables, not from TFRecord files in Cloud Storage; it cannot directly read the TFRecord format.

skills: 3.2.2: Ingesting structured and unstructured data from various sources into training pipelines.
questions.tip: Consider which approach avoids exporting data to an intermediate format while still enabling efficient batch reads for training.
questions.question:
A team is training a PyTorch tabular model on Vertex AI using a 200 GB dataset stored entirely in BigQuery. They currently export the dataset to Cloud Storage as CSV files before each training run, which takes 45 minutes and delays experimentation. They want to reduce pipeline startup time by reading the BigQuery data more directly during training without changing their PyTorch training code significantly.

Which approach MOST reduces ingestion latency compared to the current process?

choices.text: Export to Cloud Storage as Parquet instead of CSV before each training run.
choices.explanation: Exporting as Parquet instead of CSV reduces file size and read speed but still incurs the full export wait time before training can start, only marginally improving startup latency.

choices.text: Use the BigQuery Storage Read API to stream data in Arrow format directly into the training job at the start of each epoch.
choices.explanation: The Storage Read API supports parallel reading across multiple streams, which can be assigned to different DataLoader workers. The `google-cloud-bigquery-storage` client exposes data as PyArrow tables that convert directly to NumPy arrays or PyTorch tensors with minimal overhead, removing the 45-minute export step entirely.

choices.text: Set up a Cloud Pub/Sub topic and publish all 200 GB of rows as messages to be consumed by the training job.
choices.explanation: Pub/Sub is designed for low-latency streaming of individual events, not bulk transfer of 200 GB of static training data; it has per-message overhead and retention limits that make it unsuitable for this use case.

choices.text: Replicate the BigQuery table to Cloud Bigtable and read rows from Bigtable during training.
choices.explanation: Replicating to Cloud Bigtable adds engineering complexity and ongoing replication cost, and Bigtable's row-key scan pattern is not optimized for the random shuffled batch access pattern typical in ML training.

questions.explanation:
The BigQuery Storage Read API streams table data directly from BigQuery's managed storage in columnar Arrow or Avro format at high throughput, eliminating the need to export to an intermediate file format.

**Why it works:** The Storage Read API supports parallel reading across multiple streams, which can be assigned to different DataLoader workers. The `google-cloud-bigquery-storage` client exposes data as PyArrow tables that convert directly to NumPy arrays or PyTorch tensors with minimal overhead, removing the 45-minute export step entirely.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Exporting as Parquet instead of CSV reduces file size and read speed but still incurs the full export wait time before training can start, only marginally improving startup latency.
- Pub/Sub is designed for low-latency streaming of individual events, not bulk transfer of 200 GB of static training data; it has per-message overhead and retention limits that make it unsuitable for this use case.
- Replicating to Cloud Bigtable adds engineering complexity and ongoing replication cost, and Bigtable's row-key scan pattern is not optimized for the random shuffled batch access pattern typical in ML training.

skills: 3.2.2: Ingesting structured and unstructured data from various sources into training pipelines.

questions.question:
A team is building a training pipeline for a large-scale recommendation model. Raw interaction logs are stored as unstructured JSON files in Cloud Storage and are updated daily. The features require heavy preprocessing: parsing nested JSON, computing rolling statistics, and normalizing values. The team is concerned about wasting GPU time on CPU-bound data preprocessing during training.

Which TWO strategies BEST address the data ingestion and preprocessing bottleneck?

choices.text: Run a Dataflow job to preprocess the JSON logs and write output as TFRecord files to Cloud Storage before the training job starts.
choices.explanation: Running Dataflow offline converts raw JSON into optimized TFRecord format once per day, so training jobs always read pre-cleaned, normalized data without any parsing overhead. Using `tf.data` with `.map()` and `prefetch(AUTOTUNE)` allows CPU workers to preprocess the next batch in parallel while the GPU is processing the current batch, hiding I/O and CPU latency behind compute.

choices.text: Use the `tf.data` pipeline with `.map()` and `prefetch(tf.data.AUTOTUNE)` to perform preprocessing asynchronously on CPU while the GPU trains.
choices.explanation: Running Dataflow offline converts raw JSON into optimized TFRecord format once per day, so training jobs always read pre-cleaned, normalized data without any parsing overhead. Using `tf.data` with `.map()` and `prefetch(AUTOTUNE)` allows CPU workers to preprocess the next batch in parallel while the GPU is processing the current batch, hiding I/O and CPU latency behind compute.

choices.text: Read JSON files directly in the training loop using Python's built-in `json` module, parsing each record synchronously before each forward pass.
choices.explanation: Parsing JSON synchronously in the training loop blocks the GPU between every forward pass, creating a severe CPU bottleneck that underutilizes the accelerator.

choices.text: Store all JSON logs in Cloud Spanner and query them with SQL during each training step to compute rolling statistics.
choices.explanation: Cloud Spanner is a globally distributed relational database optimized for transactional OLTP workloads, not for streaming large-scale feature computation into ML training loops.

choices.text: Convert JSON files to PNG images and use a pre-built image DataLoader to ingest them during training.
choices.explanation: Converting JSON records to PNG images is a nonsensical data transformation that loses information and introduces unnecessary encoding/decoding overhead.

questions.explanation:
The two best strategies separate heavy preprocessing from GPU training time, either by materializing clean features before training starts or by overlapping preprocessing with GPU computation during training.

**Why it works:** Running Dataflow offline converts raw JSON into optimized TFRecord format once per day, so training jobs always read pre-cleaned, normalized data without any parsing overhead. Using `tf.data` with `.map()` and `prefetch(AUTOTUNE)` allows CPU workers to preprocess the next batch in parallel while the GPU is processing the current batch, hiding I/O and CPU latency behind compute.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Parsing JSON synchronously in the training loop blocks the GPU between every forward pass, creating a severe CPU bottleneck that underutilizes the accelerator.
- Cloud Spanner is a globally distributed relational database optimized for transactional OLTP workloads, not for streaming large-scale feature computation into ML training loops.
- Converting JSON records to PNG images is a nonsensical data transformation that loses information and introduces unnecessary encoding/decoding overhead.

skills: 3.2.2: Ingesting structured and unstructured data from various sources into training pipelines.
questions.question:
The team needs to ingest 800 GB of tabular training data from a BigQuery table into a distributed PyTorch training job running on Agent Platform. A team member proposes the following ingestion code.

```python
from google.cloud import bigquery
import pandas as pd

client = bigquery.Client()
query = 'SELECT * FROM `project.dataset.training_table`'
df = client.query(query).to_dataframe()
df.to_parquet('/tmp/training_data.parquet')
```

Why is this approach problematic for this workload?

choices.text: The code downloads all 800 GB into a single machine's memory using to_dataframe(), which will exhaust RAM on a standard training VM and cannot distribute data across multiple workers.
choices.explanation: to_dataframe() materialises the entire query result into a pandas DataFrame in the driver process's memory. 800 GB will exceed available RAM and cannot be split across distributed workers without additional logic.

choices.text: The BigQuery client library does not support queries containing SELECT * and requires explicit column names to export data to parquet format.
choices.explanation: The BigQuery client fully supports SELECT * queries. The problem with this code is memory exhaustion from materialising 800 GB into a single pandas DataFrame, not the query syntax.

choices.text: Writing to /tmp/training_data.parquet is not accessible by Agent Platform training workers because /tmp is a local path that does not persist across container restarts.
choices.explanation: While /tmp persistence is a valid concern, the more fundamental problem is that 800 GB cannot be loaded into memory in the first place. A persistent path issue would only arise if the load somehow succeeded.

choices.text: The parquet file format is not compatible with PyTorch DataLoader and must be converted to TFRecord format before it can be used in distributed training.
choices.explanation: PyTorch DataLoader can read parquet files using libraries like pandas or PyArrow. The format is not the issue - the memory exhaustion from loading 800 GB into a single DataFrame is the core problem.

questions.tip: Consider what happens when to_dataframe() is called on a query returning hundreds of gigabytes of data.
questions.explanation:
Calling `to_dataframe()` on a BigQuery query that returns 800 GB downloads the entire result set into a single pandas DataFrame in the local process's memory. This will exhaust RAM on any standard VM and does not distribute data across workers. The correct approach is to use the BigQuery Storage Read API with sharding, or export to Cloud Storage as sharded files, enabling each distributed worker to read its own shard.

**Why it works (correct approach):** The BigQuery Storage Read API parallelises reads directly to training workers without requiring a single-machine aggregation step.

**Why the others don't work:**
- SELECT * syntax: fully supported; not the cause.
- /tmp persistence: a secondary concern; moot if the load fails first.
- Parquet/PyTorch compatibility: parquet is fully compatible with PyTorch via pandas/PyArrow.

skills: 3.2.3: Training models using different software development kits (SDKs) (e.g., Agent Platform custom training, Kubeflow on Google Kubernetes Engine [GKE], Agent Platform AutoML, and Tabular Workflows) and organizing training on Google Cloud.
questions.tip: Focus on which SDK method is used to submit a containerized custom training job to Vertex AI.
questions.question:
A machine learning engineer has written a PyTorch training script and packaged it into a Docker container stored in Artifact Registry. They want to submit this container as a managed training job on Vertex AI so that Google Cloud handles resource provisioning, monitoring, and job lifecycle management. They are using the Vertex AI Python SDK.

Which code snippet correctly submits this custom training job?

choices.text:
```python
from google.cloud import aiplatform

aiplatform.init(project='my-project', location='us-central1')
job = aiplatform.CustomContainerTrainingJob(
    display_name='pytorch-train',
    container_uri='us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/my-project/my-repo/trainer:latest',
)
job.run(
    machine_type='n1-standard-8',
    accelerator_type='NVIDIA_TESLA_T4',
    accelerator_count=1,
)```
choices.explanation: CustomContainerTrainingJob wraps the container URI and submits it to Vertex AI's training service, which provisions the requested machine type and accelerator, streams logs to Cloud Logging, and manages the job lifecycle. This is the standard SDK pattern for bring-your-own-container custom training.

choices.text:
```python
from google.cloud import aiplatform

aiplatform.init(project='my-project', location='us-central1')
job = aiplatform.AutoMLTabularTrainingJob(
    display_name='pytorch-train',
    container_uri='us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/my-project/my-repo/trainer:latest',
)
job.run(dataset=None, target_column='label')```
choices.explanation: AutoMLTabularTrainingJob is for launching AutoML tabular training jobs, not custom containers; it requires a Vertex AI Dataset and a target column, not a container URI.

choices.text:
```python
import subprocess
subprocess.run([
    'gcloud', 'ai', 'custom-jobs', 'create',
    '--region=us-central1',
    '--display-name=pytorch-train',
    '--worker-pool-spec=machine-type=n1-standard-8,container-image-uri=gcr.io/my-project/trainer'
])```
choices.explanation: Using subprocess.run with the gcloud CLI from within Python code is brittle, bypasses SDK authentication handling, and is not the recommended SDK pattern for programmatic job submission.

choices.text:
```python
from google.cloud import aiplatform

aiplatform.init(project='my-project', location='us-central1')
job = aiplatform.PipelineJob(
    display_name='pytorch-train',
    template_path='pytorch_train_pipeline.json',
)
job.run()```
choices.explanation: PipelineJob is for running Kubeflow Pipelines or Vertex Pipelines workflows defined in a compiled pipeline JSON, not for submitting a single standalone custom training container.

questions.explanation:
`aiplatform.CustomContainerTrainingJob` is the correct Vertex AI SDK class for submitting a user-provided Docker container as a managed training job, with hardware configuration passed to `job.run()`.

**Why it works:** `CustomContainerTrainingJob` wraps the container URI and submits it to Vertex AI's training service, which provisions the requested machine type and accelerator, streams logs to Cloud Logging, and manages the job lifecycle. This is the standard SDK pattern for bring-your-own-container custom training.

**Why the others don't work:**
- `AutoMLTabularTrainingJob` is for launching AutoML tabular training jobs, not custom containers; it requires a Vertex AI Dataset and a target column, not a container URI.
- Using `subprocess.run` with the `gcloud` CLI from within Python code is brittle, bypasses SDK authentication handling, and is not the recommended SDK pattern for programmatic job submission.
- `PipelineJob` is for running Kubeflow Pipelines or Vertex Pipelines workflows defined in a compiled pipeline JSON, not for submitting a single standalone custom training container.

questions.question:
A data science platform team supports 15 ML engineers who each run independent training experiments. They want to standardize training workflows so that data preprocessing, model training, and evaluation are defined as reusable pipeline components with tracked artifact lineage. The team needs the solution to run on Google Cloud and support both CPU and GPU nodes without managing underlying Kubernetes infrastructure directly.

Which SDK and training approach BEST meets these requirements?

choices.text: Use Vertex AI Pipelines with the Kubeflow Pipelines SDK to define preprocessing, training, and evaluation as discrete pipeline components, submitted via Vertex AI's managed pipeline service.
choices.explanation: KFP components are Python functions decorated with `@component` that compile to reusable pipeline steps. Vertex AI Pipelines handles scheduling, artifact tracking in Vertex ML Metadata, and provisioning of CPU/GPU nodes for each step without the team needing to manage Kubernetes. This is the standard approach for standardizing team-wide ML workflows on Google Cloud.

choices.text: Use Vertex AI AutoML to let the platform automatically define all pipeline stages without any custom component authoring.
choices.explanation: Vertex AI AutoML does not support custom pipeline components or user-defined preprocessing logic; it is an automated training tool for standard tasks, not a general workflow orchestration system.

choices.text: Write a shell script that calls `gcloud ai custom-jobs create` sequentially for each pipeline stage and stores artifacts in Cloud Storage manually.

choices.text: Deploy self-managed Kubeflow on GKE and maintain the cluster infrastructure independently to get full control over component scheduling.
choices.explanation: Self-managed Kubeflow on GKE provides more flexibility but requires significant Kubernetes operational overhead (upgrades, node pool management, autoscaling), which contradicts the requirement of not managing infrastructure directly.

questions.explanation:

**Why it works:** KFP components are Python functions decorated with `@component` that compile to reusable pipeline steps. Vertex AI Pipelines handles scheduling, artifact tracking in Vertex ML Metadata, and provisioning of CPU/GPU nodes for each step without the team needing to manage Kubernetes. This is the standard approach for standardizing team-wide ML workflows on Google Cloud.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Vertex AI AutoML does not support custom pipeline components or user-defined preprocessing logic; it is an automated training tool for standard tasks, not a general workflow orchestration system.
- Sequential `gcloud` shell script calls provide no artifact lineage, no component reuse, no parallelism, and no failure recovery -- making them unfit for a team-wide platform.
