questions.explanation:
Vertex AI online prediction endpoints provide fully managed GPU-backed serving with automatic scaling, removing node pool and cluster management burden.

**Why it works:** Vertex AI handles infrastructure provisioning, health checks, autoscaling, and model versioning; dedicated machine types with A100 GPUs are supported, and the endpoint is designed for low-latency synchronous requests.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Cloud Run with GPU: Cloud Run GPU support is available but limited to specific GPU types; it does not support A100s and is better suited for lighter inference workloads.
- GKE Autopilot: Offers managed Kubernetes but the team still owns cluster configuration, node pool scheduling, and GPU driver management.

questions.question:
A startup wants to serve a lightweight text classification model with sporadic traffic patterns. The model receives no requests for hours at a time, then handles short bursts of hundreds of requests per minute. The team has no Kubernetes expertise and needs to minimise idle costs.

Which two serving options BEST fit these requirements? (Choose 2)

choices.text: Deploy the model to a Vertex AI online prediction endpoint configured with minimum replicas set to 0 to enable scale-to-zero.
choices.explanation: Vertex AI online prediction supports setting minimum replicas to 0, incurring no serving cost during idle periods; Cloud Run is inherently serverless and scales to zero natively, making both options ideal for sporadic workloads without Kubernetes expertise.

choices.text: Package the model server as a container and deploy it to Cloud Run, which scales to zero between bursts.
choices.explanation: Vertex AI online prediction supports setting minimum replicas to 0, incurring no serving cost during idle periods; Cloud Run is inherently serverless and scales to zero natively, making both options ideal for sporadic workloads without Kubernetes expertise.

choices.text: Create a GKE Standard cluster with a dedicated node pool and keep at least one node running at all times.
choices.explanation: GKE Standard with persistent node: Requires Kubernetes expertise and incurs continuous node costs even when idle.

choices.text: Deploy the model to a Vertex AI endpoint with a dedicated deployment resource pool to guarantee capacity.
choices.explanation: Dedicated deployment resource pool: Reserves capacity continuously, which eliminates scale-to-zero and increases idle cost.

choices.text: Run the model server on a Compute Engine VM and use a startup script to load the model on each boot.
choices.explanation: Compute Engine VM: Requires manual management, keeps the VM running (and billing) even when idle, and has no built-in autoscaling.

questions.explanation:
Vertex AI endpoints with scale-to-zero and Cloud Run both eliminate idle infrastructure costs while handling burst traffic automatically.

**Why it works:** Vertex AI online prediction supports setting minimum replicas to 0, incurring no serving cost during idle periods; Cloud Run is inherently serverless and scales to zero natively, making both options ideal for sporadic workloads without Kubernetes expertise.

**Why the others don't work:**
- GKE Standard with persistent node: Requires Kubernetes expertise and incurs continuous node costs even when idle.
- Dedicated deployment resource pool: Reserves capacity continuously, which eliminates scale-to-zero and increases idle cost.
- Compute Engine VM: Requires manual management, keeps the VM running (and billing) even when idle, and has no built-in autoscaling.

skills: 4.1.1: Deploying models for batch and online inference using appropriate services (e.g., Agent Platform, Model Garden, Cloud Run, and GKE).
questions.question:
The team needs to deploy a trained model from Agent Platform Model Registry to an online prediction endpoint. A team member writes the following SDK code.

```python
from google.cloud import aiplatform

aiplatform.init(project='my-project', location='us-central1')

model = aiplatform.Model('projects/my-project/locations/us-central1/models/1234567890')

endpoint = aiplatform.Endpoint.create(display_name='fraud-endpoint')

model.deploy(
    endpoint=endpoint,
    machine_type='n1-standard-4',
    min_replica_count=1,
    max_replica_count=5
)
```

The deployment succeeds but the endpoint scales to max_replica_count during low-traffic periods, incurring unexpected costs. What should be changed to allow the endpoint to scale down to zero replicas when there is no traffic?

choices.text: Change min_replica_count to 0 and ensure the endpoint uses a non-dedicated resource configuration, enabling scale-to-zero when the endpoint receives no requests.
choices.explanation: Setting min_replica_count=0 enables scale-to-zero on Agent Platform shared (non-dedicated) endpoints. When traffic drops to zero, the platform deallocates all replicas, eliminating idle compute cost.

choices.text: Set traffic_split={model.resource_name: 0} on the endpoint after deployment to suspend traffic routing and reduce replicas to zero automatically.
choices.explanation: traffic_split controls how traffic is distributed between model versions on an endpoint, not replica count. Setting it to 0 routes no traffic but does not deallocate the existing replicas.

choices.text: Replace aiplatform.Endpoint.create() with aiplatform.PrivateEndpoint.create() to use private endpoints, which automatically scale to zero when not in use.
choices.explanation: Private endpoints provide VPC-isolated access but do not inherently support scale-to-zero. Scale-to-zero is a feature of the min_replica_count=0 configuration on shared endpoints.

choices.text: Add autoscaling_target_resource_utilization=0 to the deploy() call to instruct the autoscaler to target zero resource utilisation and trigger scale-down.
choices.explanation: autoscaling_target_resource_utilization is not a valid parameter for model.deploy(). Scale-to-zero is controlled by min_replica_count=0, not a utilisation target.

questions.tip: Consider which deployment parameter defines the floor for replica count and how that affects idle cost.
questions.explanation:
Setting `min_replica_count=0` allows Agent Platform to scale the endpoint down to zero replicas when there is no incoming traffic, eliminating idle costs entirely. The endpoint scales back up automatically when new requests arrive (with a cold start delay).

**Why it works:** min_replica_count defines the lower bound for autoscaling. Zero enables full scale-to-zero on shared (non-dedicated) Agent Platform endpoints.

**Why the others don't work:**
- traffic_split=0: stops routing traffic but keeps replicas alive and billing.
- PrivateEndpoint: provides network isolation, not scale-to-zero capability.
- autoscaling_target_resource_utilization: not a valid deploy() parameter.

questions.question: You have trained an XGBoost 1.7 model and exported it as model.bst to Cloud Storage. You want to deploy it to a Vertex AI online endpoint with the least amount of custom code and infrastructure to manage. What should you do?

questions.explanation:
Google provides prebuilt serving container images for XGBoost that handle model loading and HTTP prediction routing without any custom code.

**Why it works:** When registering the model in Vertex AI, specifying the official prebuilt XGBoost container URI (e.g., `us-docker.pkg.dev/vertex-ai/prediction/xgboost-cpu.1-7:latest`) instructs Vertex AI to load the artifact automatically, exposing a standard prediction endpoint with zero custom server code.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Custom Flask image: Functional but unnecessary; it requires writing, testing, and maintaining a model server that the prebuilt container already provides.
- Convert to TensorFlow SavedModel: Format conversion introduces risk of accuracy drift and adds significant engineering effort for no benefit when a native XGBoost container exists.

skills: 4.1.2: Packaging and serving models from different frameworks (e.g., PyTorch and XGBoost) using prebuilt and custom containers.
questions.tip: Vertex AI tells your custom container which port and route to serve through specific environment variables; your server must honor them.
questions.question:
You are packaging a custom PyTorch model server in a Docker container for Vertex AI online prediction because your model uses a non-standard tokenizer that no prebuilt container supports. You have written the following partial Dockerfile.

```dockerfile
FROM pytorch/pytorch:2.2.0-cuda11.8-cudnn8-runtime
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY server.py .
CMD ["python", "server.py"]
```

Which additional requirement MUST your container satisfy for Vertex AI to route prediction traffic to it correctly?

choices.text: The HTTP server in server.py must listen on the port given by the AIP_HTTP_PORT environment variable (8080 by default) and expose the prediction route configured by AIP_PREDICT_ROUTE.
choices.explanation: Vertex AI sets AIP_HTTP_PORT and AIP_PREDICT_ROUTE inside the container and forwards prediction traffic accordingly. A server that hard-codes a different port or route is unreachable, regardless of how the model is built.

choices.text: The Dockerfile must rebuild from a Google-provided base image hosted in Artifact Registry; public PyTorch images are rejected by Vertex AI.
choices.explanation: Vertex AI accepts any container image it can pull, including public PyTorch images. The base image is not what blocks deployment.

choices.text: The container must respond to a GET /healthz probe within one second of startup, otherwise Vertex AI refuses to deploy it.
choices.explanation: Vertex AI does probe a health route, but the route is configured by AIP_HEALTH_ROUTE (not /healthz) and the one-second startup deadline is fabricated. This is not the binding requirement that determines whether traffic can be routed.

choices.text: The model weights must be baked into the image at build time; Vertex AI does not load model artifacts from Cloud Storage at deploy time for custom containers.
choices.explanation: Vertex AI does support loading model artifacts from a Cloud Storage URI at deploy time. Baking weights into the image is allowed but not required, and is often discouraged because of image size.

questions.explanation:
Vertex AI defines a contract for custom prediction containers through environment variables that the runtime injects, in particular AIP_HTTP_PORT, AIP_PREDICT_ROUTE, and AIP_HEALTH_ROUTE.

**Why it works:** When your server binds to the port and routes specified by these variables, Vertex AI can forward prediction requests to it. Hard-coding a different port or path means the runtime cannot reach the server, and the deployment fails its health checks.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Google-provided base image: not required; any pullable image is allowed.
- /healthz with a one-second deadline: Vertex AI uses AIP_HEALTH_ROUTE, and the timing claim is invented.
- Weights baked into the image: optional, not required; Cloud Storage artifacts are supported.

questions.question:
An ML team has retrained their fraud detection model three times over the past year. Each retraining produces a new set of model artifacts. The team wants to keep all three artifact sets discoverable and associated with the same logical model, while being able to deploy any specific version to an endpoint.

How should they structure their entries in Vertex AI Model Registry?

choices.text: Create one parent model resource named `fraud-detection` and upload each retrained artifact as a new model version under that parent.
choices.explanation: Uploading each retrained artifact as a model version under a single parent keeps versions linked, enables side-by-side comparison, and allows any version to be individually deployed or aliased without losing history.

choices.text: Create three separate top-level model resources with names `fraud-detection-v1`, `fraud-detection-v2`, and `fraud-detection-v3`.
choices.explanation: Three separate top-level resources: Creates unrelated model entries with no shared lineage; makes it harder to compare versions or track the model's evolution.

choices.text: Store all three artifact sets in the same Cloud Storage path and register a single model resource pointing to that path.
choices.explanation: Single Cloud Storage path with overwriting: A single path cannot store distinct artifacts for each version; previous artifacts would be overwritten or co-mingled.

choices.text: Create one model resource and overwrite its artifact path each time a new version is trained.
choices.explanation: Overwriting the artifact path: Destroys the ability to redeploy or audit previous versions; the registry entry loses its history.

questions.explanation:
Vertex AI Model Registry supports a parent model / model version hierarchy specifically designed to group iterations of the same logical model.

**Why it works:** Uploading each retrained artifact as a model version under a single parent keeps versions linked, enables side-by-side comparison, and allows any version to be individually deployed or aliased without losing history.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Three separate top-level resources: Creates unrelated model entries with no shared lineage; makes it harder to compare versions or track the model's evolution.
- Single Cloud Storage path with overwriting: A single path cannot store distinct artifacts for each version; previous artifacts would be overwritten or co-mingled.
- Overwriting the artifact path: Destroys the ability to redeploy or audit previous versions; the registry entry loses its history.

questions.question: Your platform team manages a production NLP model through Vertex AI Model Registry. The deployment pipeline references a model version alias called champion to determine which version is deployed to production. When a new version passes evaluation, you need to promote it to production without changing any pipeline configuration files. What should you do in Model Registry?

choices.text: Reassign the `champion` alias to point to the newly approved model version.
choices.explanation: Moving the `champion` alias to the new version causes every downstream reference to `champion` to resolve to the new version automatically, with no pipeline file changes required.

choices.text: Delete the current `champion` version and re-upload the new artifacts under the same version ID.
choices.explanation: Delete and re-upload: Deleting a version destroys its metadata and audit trail; re-uploading under the same ID is not supported.

choices.text: Create a new model resource named `champion` and copy the new version's artifacts into it.
choices.explanation: New model resource named `champion`: Creates a completely separate registry entry unrelated to the existing parent model's version history.

choices.text: Update all pipeline configuration files to reference the new version ID directly, then redeploy.
choices.explanation: Update pipeline configuration files: Defeats the purpose of using a stable alias; requires coordinated changes across all pipeline definitions each time a promotion occurs.

questions.explanation:
Aliases in Vertex AI Model Registry are mutable labels that can be reassigned to any version; updating the alias is the intended promotion mechanism.

**Why it works:** Moving the `champion` alias to the new version causes every downstream reference to `champion` to resolve to the new version automatically, with no pipeline file changes required.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Delete and re-upload: Deleting a version destroys its metadata and audit trail; re-uploading under the same ID is not supported.
- New model resource named `champion`: Creates a completely separate registry entry unrelated to the existing parent model's version history.
- Update pipeline configuration files: Defeats the purpose of using a stable alias; requires coordinated changes across all pipeline definitions each time a promotion occurs.

questions.question:
An organisation runs dozens of models across multiple business units in a single Google Cloud project. The MLOps team wants to use Vertex AI Model Registry to make models easier to discover and to enforce governance. They need to filter models by team and compliance status without relying on naming conventions.

Which two practices BEST support these organisational goals in Model Registry? (Choose 2)

choices.text: Apply resource labels (key-value pairs) to each model resource to tag attributes such as team name, compliance tier, and data classification.
choices.explanation: Resource labels are indexed and can be used in `gcloud ai models list --filter` queries; version-level metadata fields allow storing arbitrary key-value data such as evaluation metrics, enabling governance workflows to query and act on model state programmatically.

choices.text: Store structured metadata about each model version using the `labels` or `metadata` fields on the model version resource to capture training run details and evaluation metrics.
choices.explanation: Resource labels are indexed and can be used in `gcloud ai models list --filter` queries; version-level metadata fields allow storing arbitrary key-value data such as evaluation metrics, enabling governance workflows to query and act on model state programmatically.

choices.text: Encode all governance information into the model resource display name using a fixed delimiter convention.
choices.explanation: Display name encoding: Name-based conventions are fragile, hard to query programmatically, and cannot be filtered natively by the Model Registry API.

choices.text: Create a separate Google Cloud project for each team and register models only within that team's project.

questions.explanation:
Labels on model resources and metadata fields on model versions provide structured, queryable attributes that support filtering and governance without encoding information into names.

**Why it works:** Resource labels are indexed and can be used in `gcloud ai models list --filter` queries; version-level metadata fields allow storing arbitrary key-value data such as evaluation metrics, enabling governance workflows to query and act on model state programmatically.

**Why the others don't work:**

skills: 4.1.4: Implementing model rollout strategies (e.g., A/B testing and canary deployments) to compare model versions.
questions.tip: Vertex AI endpoints can host multiple deployed models simultaneously and split incoming traffic between them by percentage.
questions.question:
A product team has trained a new recommendation model and wants to compare it against the current production model before full rollout. They need 10% of live traffic to go to the new model and 90% to remain with the existing model, so they can monitor key metrics side by side.

How should they configure the Vertex AI endpoint?

choices.text: Deploy both models to the same endpoint and configure the traffic split so the existing model receives 90% and the new model receives 10%.
choices.explanation: Deploying both models to the same endpoint and setting the traffic split to 90/10 routes live production traffic proportionally, enabling real-time metric comparison without any external load balancer.

choices.text: Create two separate endpoints, one per model, and use a Cloud Load Balancing weighted backend service to split traffic.
choices.explanation: Two endpoints with Cloud Load Balancing: Adds unnecessary infrastructure complexity; traffic splitting is a first-class feature of a single Vertex AI endpoint.

choices.text: Deploy only the new model to the endpoint and set its minimum replica count to 10% of the existing model's capacity.
choices.explanation: Replica count percentage: Replica count controls capacity, not traffic distribution; traffic percentages are a separate endpoint configuration.

choices.text: Deploy the new model to a staging endpoint and manually copy 10% of the production request logs to replay against it offline.
choices.explanation: Offline log replay: Does not expose the new model to real traffic; latency, error rates, and business metrics cannot be measured accurately from replayed logs.

questions.explanation:
Vertex AI online prediction endpoints natively support traffic splitting across multiple deployed model versions using integer percentages that must sum to 100.

**Why it works:** Deploying both models to the same endpoint and setting the traffic split to 90/10 routes live production traffic proportionally, enabling real-time metric comparison without any external load balancer.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Two endpoints with Cloud Load Balancing: Adds unnecessary infrastructure complexity; traffic splitting is a first-class feature of a single Vertex AI endpoint.
- Replica count percentage: Replica count controls capacity, not traffic distribution; traffic percentages are a separate endpoint configuration.
- Offline log replay: Does not expose the new model to real traffic; latency, error rates, and business metrics cannot be measured accurately from replayed logs.

skills: 4.1.4: Implementing model rollout strategies (e.g., A/B testing and canary deployments) to compare model versions.
questions.tip: Vertex AI endpoints support an in-place traffic split between deployed model versions, which is the lowest-friction way to canary and roll back.
questions.question: Your team is rolling out a new version of a high-stakes credit scoring model. The rollout policy requires 5% of traffic for 48 hours, then 25% for another 48 hours, and only 100% after the previous stages show no degradation in precision and latency. If a stage fails, the previous model must be fully restored within minutes. You want to implement this on Vertex AI with the lowest operational complexity. What should you do?

choices.text: Deploy the new model version to the same Vertex AI endpoint as the current model and adjust the endpoint's traffic split from 5/95 to 25/75 to 100/0 between stages; on failure, set the split back to 0/100.
choices.explanation: Both versions stay deployed on one endpoint throughout the rollout. Traffic splits update through a single API call, and reverting to 0/100 instantly routes all traffic back to the previous model with no redeployment delay.

choices.text: Provision a separate Vertex AI endpoint for each rollout stage and shift traffic between endpoints by updating Cloud DNS records that the prediction client resolves.
choices.explanation: DNS TTLs introduce propagation delays of minutes to hours, which violates the requirement to fully restore the previous model within minutes, and Vertex AI's native traffic split is bypassed.

choices.text: Deploy the new model to a separate endpoint and mirror all production requests to it as shadow traffic, comparing responses offline before promoting it.
choices.explanation: Shadow mode validates outputs without exposing real users to the new model, so it cannot satisfy a policy that explicitly routes 5% and then 25% of live traffic to the new version.

choices.text: Undeploy the existing model from the endpoint and deploy the new model in its place; if a stage fails, redeploy the previous version from the Vertex AI Model Registry.
choices.explanation: Undeploying and redeploying takes minutes per cycle, leaving the endpoint in a degraded state during rollback and providing no traffic split for staged exposure.

questions.explanation:
Adjusting the traffic split on a single Vertex AI endpoint that hosts both model versions is the canonical canary pattern and the one with the smallest blast radius for rollback.

**Why it works:** Both models remain deployed throughout the rollout, so each stage transition (5/95, 25/75, 100/0) is a lightweight API update. If a stage fails, setting the split back to 0/100 fully restores the previous model in seconds without any redeployment.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Per-stage endpoints with DNS shifts: DNS propagation delays prevent minute-level rollback.
- Shadow traffic: does not expose real users, so it cannot fulfill a percentage-based traffic split policy.
- Undeploy and redeploy: rollback requires a full redeployment cycle, which violates the quick-restore requirement.

skills: 4.1.4: Implementing model rollout strategies (e.g., A/B testing and canary deployments) to compare model versions.

questions.question:
A team is running an A/B test on a Vertex AI endpoint with 20% traffic going to the challenger model and 80% to the champion. They need to decide whether to promote the challenger after one week. Their evaluation criteria are prediction latency and a custom business metric (revenue per request) computed from request logs.

Which two actions BEST support a rigorous comparison between the two models? (Choose 2)

choices.text: Configure Cloud Monitoring dashboards with metrics filtered by the deployed model ID to compare latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99) for each model separately.
choices.explanation: Vertex AI exposes per-deployed-model metrics in Cloud Monitoring, enabling side-by-side latency comparison. Request-response logging captures input and output payloads, which can be joined with business outcome data in BigQuery to compute revenue per request for each model ID.

choices.text: Export prediction request and response payloads to BigQuery using Vertex AI request-response logging, then compute revenue per request for each model version in a query.
choices.explanation: Vertex AI exposes per-deployed-model metrics in Cloud Monitoring, enabling side-by-side latency comparison. Request-response logging captures input and output payloads, which can be joined with business outcome data in BigQuery to compute revenue per request for each model ID.

choices.text: Increase the challenger's traffic split to 50% immediately to collect more data faster, regardless of current metric trends.
choices.explanation: Increasing traffic immediately: Prematurely shifting traffic before trends are established can expose more users to a potentially underperforming model and invalidates the staged evaluation plan.

choices.text: Compare the two models only on offline evaluation datasets rather than live traffic metrics to ensure consistency.
choices.explanation: Offline datasets only: Offline metrics do not capture production distribution shift, latency under real load, or the business metric the team cares about.

choices.text: Use the same endpoint URL for both models but route specific users to the challenger by embedding the model version ID in the client application.
choices.explanation: Client-side routing by version ID: Bypasses the endpoint traffic split, breaks the randomised assignment needed for a valid A/B test, and introduces selection bias.

questions.explanation:
Per-model latency metrics in Cloud Monitoring and request-response logging to BigQuery together provide the latency and business metric signals needed to make a statistically sound promotion decision.

**Why it works:** Vertex AI exposes per-deployed-model metrics in Cloud Monitoring, enabling side-by-side latency comparison. Request-response logging captures input and output payloads, which can be joined with business outcome data in BigQuery to compute revenue per request for each model ID.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Increasing traffic immediately: Prematurely shifting traffic before trends are established can expose more users to a potentially underperforming model and invalidates the staged evaluation plan.
- Offline datasets only: Offline metrics do not capture production distribution shift, latency under real load, or the business metric the team cares about.
- Client-side routing by version ID: Bypasses the endpoint traffic split, breaks the randomised assignment needed for a valid A/B test, and introduces selection bias.

skills: 4.1.4: Implementing model rollout strategies (e.g., A/B testing and canary deployments) to compare model versions.
questions.question:
The team has deployed model v1 to an existing endpoint and wants to route 10% of live traffic to model v2 as a canary deployment while keeping 90% on v1. A team member writes the following SDK code.

```python
from google.cloud import aiplatform

aiplatform.init(project='my-project', location='us-central1')

endpoint = aiplatform.Endpoint('projects/my-project/locations/us-central1/endpoints/9876543210')

model_v2 = aiplatform.Model('projects/my-project/locations/us-central1/models/1111111111')

endpoint.deploy(
    model=model_v2,
    machine_type='n1-standard-4',
    traffic_percentage=10
)
```

What does setting `traffic_percentage=10` in this deploy call accomplish?

choices.text: It deploys model v2 and adjusts the endpoint's traffic split so that 10% of prediction requests are routed to v2 and the remaining 90% continue to route to v1.
choices.explanation: traffic_percentage in endpoint.deploy() sets the fraction of traffic to direct to the newly deployed model. Agent Platform automatically adjusts the split for existing deployed models to preserve the total at 100%.

choices.text: It deploys model v2 but does not activate traffic routing; a separate endpoint.update_traffic_split() call with {'v2_id': 10, 'v1_id': 90} is still required.
choices.explanation: traffic_percentage in deploy() does set the traffic split at deployment time. A separate update_traffic_split() call is not required, though it can be used for post-deployment adjustments.

choices.text: It throttles the number of requests model v2 can handle to 10% of the endpoint's maximum throughput, reverting excess requests to v1 when v2 is saturated.
choices.explanation: traffic_percentage is a routing fraction, not a capacity cap. It defines what percentage of all incoming requests are directed to this model version, not a maximum throughput limit.

choices.text: It reserves 10% of the endpoint's compute replicas for model v2, reducing v1's replica pool to 90% of its original count to maintain the same total resource allocation.
choices.explanation: traffic_percentage controls request routing, not replica allocation. Both models have their own independently configured replica pools; the split affects which model handles each request.

questions.tip: Consider what traffic_percentage represents in terms of request routing, not compute allocation.
questions.explanation:
`traffic_percentage=10` in `endpoint.deploy()` configures the traffic split at deployment time, directing 10% of all incoming prediction requests to model v2. Agent Platform automatically reduces v1's share to 90% to keep the total at 100%. This implements a canary deployment pattern without any additional API calls.

**Why it works:** Agent Platform's endpoint traffic splitting is defined as percentages across all deployed models. Setting a value at deploy time is equivalent to calling update_traffic_split explicitly.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Separate update_traffic_split: not required; traffic_percentage handles it at deploy time.
- Throughput throttle: traffic_percentage routes requests, not caps throughput.
- Replica allocation: each model has its own replica pool; traffic split only affects routing.

skills: 4.1.5: Developing solutions for inference preprocessing and postprocessing.
questions.tip: Preprocessing that must happen inside the serving path at request time is best placed in the model server or a custom prediction routine, not in the client.
questions.question:
A team has trained an image classification model that expects input tensors normalised to the range [0, 1] with shape (224, 224, 3). Clients submit raw JPEG images as base64-encoded strings. The team does not want to modify client code to perform normalisation.

Where is the BEST place to implement the decoding and normalisation logic?

choices.text: Implement the preprocessing logic inside a custom prediction routine or custom container that decodes and normalises the image before passing it to the model.
choices.explanation: When the preprocessing lives in the serving container, clients send raw images and receive predictions without any knowledge of tensor formats or normalisation constants. The serving layer handles the transformation transparently and consistently.

choices.text: Require clients to decode and normalise images before sending requests, and document this requirement in the API spec.
choices.explanation: Require client preprocessing: Shifts responsibility to every client, creates multiple points of inconsistency, and requires coordinated updates if preprocessing logic changes.

choices.text: Run a separate preprocessing Cloud Function that clients must call before sending data to the prediction endpoint.
choices.explanation: Separate Cloud Function: Adds a network hop, increases latency and cost, and requires clients to call two services; it also creates a new failure point outside the endpoint.

choices.text: Bake the normalisation into the model's training data pipeline and rely on the model to handle unnormalised inputs at inference time.
choices.explanation: Rely on the model for unnormalised inputs: A model trained on normalised data will produce degraded predictions on unnormalised inputs; the model cannot correct for missing preprocessing.

questions.explanation:
A custom prediction routine or custom container places preprocessing inside the serving path, decoupling the client from implementation details.

**Why it works:** When the preprocessing lives in the serving container, clients send raw images and receive predictions without any knowledge of tensor formats or normalisation constants. The serving layer handles the transformation transparently and consistently.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Require client preprocessing: Shifts responsibility to every client, creates multiple points of inconsistency, and requires coordinated updates if preprocessing logic changes.
- Separate Cloud Function: Adds a network hop, increases latency and cost, and requires clients to call two services; it also creates a new failure point outside the endpoint.
- Rely on the model for unnormalised inputs: A model trained on normalised data will produce degraded predictions on unnormalised inputs; the model cannot correct for missing preprocessing.

skills: 4.1.5: Developing solutions for inference preprocessing and postprocessing.
questions.tip: Decoupling the business rule layer from the model artifact lets you redeploy rules without touching the model endpoint.

choices.text: Implement the postprocessing in a Cloud Run service that wraps the Vertex AI endpoint; clients call Cloud Run, which calls the endpoint and applies the business rules before responding.
choices.explanation: Cloud Run services can be redeployed in seconds with updated logic or configuration. The Vertex AI endpoint serving the model artifact remains unchanged, preserving model versioning and audit history while the rule layer evolves independently.

choices.text: Embed the business rules directly in the model's output layer so the model returns labels instead of scores.
choices.explanation: Embed rules in the model output layer: Requires retraining and redeployment of the model every time thresholds change, which is heavyweight and ties business logic to the ML training pipeline.

choices.text: Update the custom prediction routine container each time rules change and redeploy the model to the Vertex AI endpoint.
choices.explanation: Redeploy the custom prediction routine: Still requires a container build and endpoint redeployment cycle, which is slower and more tightly coupled than a separate Cloud Run service.

choices.text: Store the thresholds in an environment variable on the Vertex AI endpoint and restart the endpoint to pick up changes.
choices.explanation: Environment variable on the endpoint: Vertex AI online prediction endpoints do not support hot-reload of environment variables; changing them requires a new deployment.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud Run wrapper service decouples the business rule layer from the model, allowing quarterly rule updates with a Cloud Run redeployment that does not touch the model artifact or endpoint.

**Why it works:** Cloud Run services can be redeployed in seconds with updated logic or configuration. The Vertex AI endpoint serving the model artifact remains unchanged, preserving model versioning and audit history while the rule layer evolves independently.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Embed rules in the model output layer: Requires retraining and redeployment of the model every time thresholds change, which is heavyweight and ties business logic to the ML training pipeline.
- Redeploy the custom prediction routine: Still requires a container build and endpoint redeployment cycle, which is slower and more tightly coupled than a separate Cloud Run service.
- Environment variable on the endpoint: Vertex AI online prediction endpoints do not support hot-reload of environment variables; changing them requires a new deployment.

skills: 4.1.5: Developing solutions for inference preprocessing and postprocessing.
questions.tip: Feature Store online serving provides low-latency feature lookup at inference time; custom containers can call it during the preprocessing step.
questions.question:
A recommendation system retrieves user features from Vertex AI Feature Store during online inference. The serving pipeline must: (1) look up the user's feature vector from Feature Store using the user ID in the request, and (2) concatenate it with item features from the request payload before calling the model. The team wants to keep this logic server-side and avoid adding it to the client.

Which two implementation approaches are valid for server-side inference preprocessing in this scenario? (Choose 2)

choices.text: Implement the Feature Store lookup and feature concatenation in a custom prediction routine that overrides the `preprocess` method of the model server.
choices.explanation: A custom prediction routine runs inside the Vertex AI serving container and can call Feature Store's online serving API synchronously during `preprocess`. A Cloud Run proxy acts as an aggregation layer that performs the same lookup and assembly before forwarding to the endpoint, giving an alternative that is easy to update independently.

choices.text: Deploy a Cloud Run service as a preprocessing proxy that calls Vertex AI Feature Store's online serving API, concatenates features, and forwards the assembled payload to the Vertex AI prediction endpoint.
choices.explanation: A custom prediction routine runs inside the Vertex AI serving container and can call Feature Store's online serving API synchronously during `preprocess`. A Cloud Run proxy acts as an aggregation layer that performs the same lookup and assembly before forwarding to the endpoint, giving an alternative that is easy to update independently.

choices.text: Perform the Feature Store lookup inside the model training code so that the trained weights already encode user feature embeddings, eliminating the need for runtime lookup.
choices.explanation: Client-side Feature Store call: Moves complexity to the client, violating the server-side requirement and creating multiple integration points that must be kept in sync.

choices.text: Cache the entire Feature Store in Cloud Storage and read the user feature file at inference time from within the serving container.
choices.explanation: Cloud Storage file read: Cloud Storage object reads at inference time are not designed for low-latency per-request access; Feature Store's online serving is optimised for millisecond lookups.

choices.text: Require the client application to call Feature Store, assemble the feature vector, and include it in the prediction request payload.
choices.explanation: Training-time embedding: Baking user features into model weights at training time means the model cannot reflect feature changes without retraining; it also does not support real-time personalisation.

questions.explanation:
Both a custom prediction routine and a Cloud Run preprocessing proxy keep the Feature Store lookup server-side, satisfying the requirement to shield clients from this logic.

**Why it works:** A custom prediction routine runs inside the Vertex AI serving container and can call Feature Store's online serving API synchronously during `preprocess`. A Cloud Run proxy acts as an aggregation layer that performs the same lookup and assembly before forwarding to the endpoint, giving an alternative that is easy to update independently.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Training-time embedding: Baking user features into model weights at training time means the model cannot reflect feature changes without retraining; it also does not support real-time personalisation.
- Cloud Storage file read: Cloud Storage object reads at inference time are not designed for low-latency per-request access; Feature Store's online serving is optimised for millisecond lookups.
- Client-side Feature Store call: Moves complexity to the client, violating the server-side requirement and creating multiple integration points that must be kept in sync.

skills: 4.1.5: Developing solutions for inference preprocessing and postprocessing.

choices.text: The normalisation statistics were not saved to the model artifact directory alongside the sklearn model file, so they are unavailable when the predictor loads the model at serving time.
choices.explanation: Custom Prediction Routines load artifacts from the model directory. The load() class method must read any saved statistics (e.g., mean_ and std_) from files in the artifact directory and set them as instance attributes. Without this, they are undefined at serving time.

choices.text: SklearnPredictor automatically zeroes any attribute not defined in its base class at container startup, so mean_ and std_ are reset to 0 before preprocess is called.
choices.explanation: SklearnPredictor does not zero or restrict user-defined attributes. The issue is that mean_ and std_ were never loaded from the artifact directory in the first place.

choices.text: The preprocess method must call super().preprocess() first to initialise base class attributes, which triggers the load of mean_ and std_ as part of the SklearnPredictor initialisation sequence.
choices.explanation: The base preprocess method handles base class concerns only. It does not load user-defined statistics. An explicit load() override is required to read these values from the artifact directory.

choices.text: The normalisation statistics must be recomputed inside preprocess on each request batch by fitting a StandardScaler on the incoming instances before applying the transform.
choices.explanation: Recomputing statistics on each request batch would apply serving-time statistics rather than training-time statistics, introducing training-serving skew. Statistics must be loaded from the training artifact.

questions.tip: Consider how a Custom Prediction Routine accesses state that was computed during training - where must that state be stored and loaded from?
questions.explanation:
A Custom Prediction Routine loads model artifacts from the directory pointed to by the model artifact URI. The normalisation statistics (mean_, std_) must be serialised (e.g., as a numpy file or JSON) to that directory during training, then loaded in an overridden `load()` class method that sets `self.mean_` and `self.std_`. Without a `load()` override that reads these files, the attributes are undefined at serving time.

**Why it works:** Overriding `load()` to read saved statistics from the artifact directory restores the serving-time state that was computed during training.

**Why the others don't work:**
- SklearnPredictor attribute restriction: the base class does not restrict custom attributes; the issue is loading, not definition.
- super().preprocess(): the base class preprocess does not initialise user-defined statistics.
- Per-request computation: normalisation must use training statistics, not per-request data.

skills: 4.2.1: Managing and serving features using Agent Platform Feature Store.
questions.tip: Online inference at single-digit millisecond latency requires a key-value online serving path, not a query against the offline source.
questions.question: Your team is building a real-time product recommendation service. User features such as click history and cart contents are computed daily in BigQuery and must be retrieved within 10 ms during online inference. You want to serve these features through Vertex AI Feature Store while minimizing serving latency and operational overhead. What should you do?

choices.text: Create a Feature Group sourced from the BigQuery table and configure a Feature Online Store with a Feature View that syncs from the Feature Group on a daily schedule.
choices.explanation: The Feature Online Store is the low-latency serving path. A Feature View materializes the latest values from the BigQuery-backed Feature Group into a key-value store optimized for sub-10 ms reads.

choices.text: Register a Feature Group on the BigQuery table and have the recommendation service issue a BigQuery query for each prediction request.
choices.explanation: Direct BigQuery queries take hundreds of milliseconds to seconds and are billed per query, so they cannot meet a 10 ms online latency budget.

choices.text: Export the BigQuery features to Parquet files in Cloud Storage and have the model read them at request time through a Cloud Storage FUSE mount.
choices.explanation: Cloud Storage is an offline object store; FUSE-mounted Parquet reads add seconds of object fetch latency and provide no key-based lookup.

choices.text: Create a Vertex AI Dataset linked to the BigQuery table and configure the deployed model endpoint to read the dataset for every prediction.
choices.explanation: Vertex AI Datasets are a training-time abstraction for managing labeled data; they do not provide an online feature retrieval path at inference time.

questions.explanation:
Vertex AI Feature Store separates an offline source (the Feature Group, often backed by BigQuery) from a low-latency online serving layer (the Feature Online Store).

**Why it works:** A Feature View materializes the latest values from the Feature Group into the Online Store on a defined schedule. The recommendation service then issues key-based reads against the Online Store, achieving the single-digit millisecond latency required for online inference.

**Why the others don't work:**
- BigQuery at request time: query latency is far above 10 ms and costs scale with traffic.
- Cloud Storage Parquet via FUSE: an offline access pattern with no key-based lookup; latency is seconds, not milliseconds.
- Vertex AI Dataset: manages training data; it is not an online feature serving mechanism.

skills: 4.2.1: Managing and serving features using Agent Platform Feature Store.
questions.tip: Consider what happens to the Feature Online Store when the sync schedule interval and the model serving SLA are not aligned.
questions.question:
An ML team has deployed a fraud detection model that reads features from a Vertex AI Feature Online Store at inference time. The underlying Feature Group sources from a BigQuery table that is updated by a streaming pipeline every 5 minutes. The Feature View sync is configured to run once per hour. A security audit finds that during a 45-minute window after a high-risk transaction pattern appears in BigQuery, the online store still serves stale feature values.

What is the MOST direct configuration change to reduce feature staleness for this use case?

choices.text: Decrease the Feature View sync interval to run every 5 minutes so that the online store reflects updates shortly after they land in BigQuery.
choices.explanation: Reducing the sync interval to 5 minutes means the Feature Online Store will be at most 5 minutes behind BigQuery, aligning with the upstream pipeline cadence and dramatically shrinking the staleness window.

choices.text: Replace the Feature Online Store with a Vertex AI Dataset and query BigQuery directly from the model endpoint at inference time.
choices.explanation: Direct BigQuery query at inference: Bypasses the low-latency online store and introduces unacceptable query latency for real-time fraud detection.

choices.text: Enable continuous materialization on the Feature Group so that BigQuery runs a scheduled export to Cloud Storage hourly.
choices.explanation: Continuous materialization to Cloud Storage: This is an offline pattern; it does not affect the Feature Online Store or its sync behavior.

choices.text: Increase the BigQuery streaming pipeline throughput to write rows faster, which automatically reduces the online store sync lag.
choices.explanation: Increasing pipeline throughput: Upstream write speed does not alter how frequently the Feature View pulls data from BigQuery into the online store.

questions.explanation:
The Feature View sync interval is the configuration knob that controls how frequently the online store pulls updated values from the BigQuery source.

**Why it works:** Reducing the sync interval to 5 minutes means the Feature Online Store will be at most 5 minutes behind BigQuery, aligning with the upstream pipeline cadence and dramatically shrinking the staleness window.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Direct BigQuery query at inference: Bypasses the low-latency online store and introduces unacceptable query latency for real-time fraud detection.
- Continuous materialization to Cloud Storage: This is an offline pattern; it does not affect the Feature Online Store or its sync behavior.
- Increasing pipeline throughput: Upstream write speed does not alter how frequently the Feature View pulls data from BigQuery into the online store.

skills: 4.2.1: Managing and serving features using Agent Platform Feature Store.
questions.tip: Think about the two distinct resource types you must provision before online feature serving is possible.
questions.question:
A data engineering team is setting up Vertex AI Feature Store for a new personalization service. They have already created Feature Groups backed by BigQuery tables. Before the model endpoint can call `FetchFeatureValues` to retrieve online features, the team needs to complete the provisioning of the serving infrastructure.

Which two steps must the team complete to enable online feature serving? (Choose 2)

choices.text: Create a Feature Online Store specifying the backend type (Bigtable or Optimized) and the desired node count or capacity.
choices.explanation: The Feature Online Store allocates the low-latency serving infrastructure. The Feature View declares which features from which Feature Groups are materialized into that store and initiates the sync from BigQuery.

choices.text: Create a Feature View within the Feature Online Store that maps the Feature Group and its features, then trigger an initial sync.
choices.explanation: The Feature Online Store allocates the low-latency serving infrastructure. The Feature View declares which features from which Feature Groups are materialized into that store and initiates the sync from BigQuery.

choices.text: Export the Feature Group data to a Cloud Storage bucket in TFRecord format so the model can load features during startup.
choices.explanation: Cloud Storage TFRecord export: An offline batch serving pattern; it is not used by the online serving API.

choices.text: Register the Feature Online Store as a Vertex AI Endpoint serving container using the Custom Container deployment flow.
choices.explanation: Registering as a Vertex AI Endpoint container: Feature Store has its own serving API; it is not deployed as a custom container endpoint.

choices.text: Enable the Vertex AI Training API on the project to allow the feature store to access BigQuery source tables.
choices.explanation: Enabling Training API: Feature retrieval uses the Vertex AI Feature Store API, not the Training API; BigQuery access is governed by IAM, not this API flag.

questions.explanation:
Online serving in Vertex AI Feature Store requires provisioning the storage backend (Feature Online Store) and defining the data projection (Feature View) before `FetchFeatureValues` calls will succeed.

**Why it works:** The Feature Online Store allocates the low-latency serving infrastructure. The Feature View declares which features from which Feature Groups are materialized into that store and initiates the sync from BigQuery.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Cloud Storage TFRecord export: An offline batch serving pattern; it is not used by the online serving API.
- Registering as a Vertex AI Endpoint container: Feature Store has its own serving API; it is not deployed as a custom container endpoint.
- Enabling Training API: Feature retrieval uses the Vertex AI Feature Store API, not the Training API; BigQuery access is governed by IAM, not this API flag.

skills: 4.2.1: Managing and serving features using Agent Platform Feature Store.
questions.tip: Each Feature Store concept maps to a distinct responsibility in the data-to-serving pipeline.
questions.question:
A team is learning the Vertex AI Feature Store object model. They need to understand which resource is responsible for each part of the feature management lifecycle.

Match each Feature Store concept to its primary responsibility.

slots.label: Feature Group
Feature
Feature Online Store
Feature View

choices.text: A logical resource backed by a BigQuery table or view that acts as the authoritative source of feature data.
choices.explanation: The Feature Group is the logical resource backed by a BigQuery table or view that acts as the authoritative offline source of feature data for downstream consumers.

choices.text: A named column within a Feature Group that represents a single measurable attribute of an entity.
choices.explanation: A Feature is a named column within a Feature Group representing a single measurable attribute of an entity such as a user or a product.

choices.text: A provisioned low-latency backend (Bigtable or Optimized) that stores materialized feature values for online reads.
choices.explanation: The Feature Online Store is the provisioned low-latency backend (Bigtable or Optimized) that stores materialized feature values for online reads at single-digit millisecond latency.

choices.text: A projection definition within an online store that specifies which Feature Group columns to sync and serve.
choices.explanation: A Feature View is a projection inside an online store that specifies which Feature Group columns to sync and serve, including the sync schedule.

choices.text: A scheduled export job that moves feature data from BigQuery to Cloud Storage for batch training pipelines.
choices.explanation: Scheduled Cloud Storage exports are not part of the Feature Store object model; this distractor describes a generic ETL job, not a Feature Store resource.

questions.explanation:
Vertex AI Feature Store uses a four-level hierarchy: Feature Group (BigQuery source) contains Features (individual columns); the Feature Online Store (Bigtable/Optimized backend) hosts Feature Views (data projections with sync schedules).

**Why it works:** This separation of concerns lets teams define features once in BigQuery and serve them both offline (via the Feature Group/BigQuery layer) and online (via Feature Views materialized into the Feature Online Store) without duplicating logic.

skills: 4.2.2: Deploying models to public and private endpoints.
questions.tip: Think about which endpoint type keeps traffic entirely within Google's network and never exposes a public IP.
questions.question:
A healthcare company is deploying a diagnostic ML model on Vertex AI. Regulatory requirements state that inference traffic must never traverse the public internet, and the model endpoint must only be reachable from within the company's VPC network.

Which endpoint configuration satisfies these requirements?

choices.text: Deploy the model to a Vertex AI private endpoint configured with Private Service Connect, accessible only from the specified VPC.
choices.explanation: Private Service Connect creates a private IP in the customer's VPC that forwards requests to the Vertex AI serving infrastructure. Traffic is fully contained within Google's network, satisfying the no-public-internet requirement.

choices.text: Deploy the model to a public Vertex AI endpoint and restrict access using an API key stored in Secret Manager.
choices.explanation: Public endpoint with API key: The endpoint still has a public IP; traffic traverses the internet even if protected by a key.

choices.text: Deploy the model to a public Vertex AI endpoint and configure a Cloud Armor security policy to allowlist only the company's egress IP.
choices.explanation: Cloud Armor allowlist: Cloud Armor operates at the HTTP layer in front of a public endpoint; the endpoint remains internet-accessible and traffic still crosses the public internet.

choices.text: Deploy the model to a shared Vertex AI endpoint and use VPC firewall rules to block inbound traffic from the internet.
choices.explanation: Shared endpoint with firewall rules: Shared (public) endpoints do not support VPC-level firewall enforcement; the endpoint IP is publicly routable.

questions.explanation:
Vertex AI private endpoints use Private Service Connect to route all inference traffic over Google's internal network, never assigning a public IP to the endpoint.

**Why it works:** Private Service Connect creates a private IP in the customer's VPC that forwards requests to the Vertex AI serving infrastructure. Traffic is fully contained within Google's network, satisfying the no-public-internet requirement.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Public endpoint with API key: The endpoint still has a public IP; traffic traverses the internet even if protected by a key.
- Cloud Armor allowlist: Cloud Armor operates at the HTTP layer in front of a public endpoint; the endpoint remains internet-accessible and traffic still crosses the public internet.
- Shared endpoint with firewall rules: Shared (public) endpoints do not support VPC-level firewall enforcement; the endpoint IP is publicly routable.

skills: 4.2.2: Deploying models to public and private endpoints.
questions.tip: Consider the connectivity mechanism that distinguishes VPC peering from Private Service Connect when choosing a private endpoint strategy.
questions.question:
An ML platform team is evaluating two options for exposing a Vertex AI model endpoint privately. Option A uses VPC Network Peering between the Vertex AI service project and the consumer VPC. Option B uses Private Service Connect (PSC) with a forwarding rule in the consumer VPC. The team needs the endpoint to be accessible from multiple consumer VPCs without creating overlapping IP range conflicts.

Which option BEST meets this requirement and why?

choices.text: Option B (PSC), because Private Service Connect creates a private IP endpoint in each consumer VPC independently, avoiding the transitive routing and IP overlap constraints imposed by VPC peering.
choices.explanation: Each consumer VPC creates its own PSC forwarding rule with a locally assigned IP. VPCs do not need to have non-overlapping ranges with each other or with the service producer, and peering is not required between consumer VPCs.

choices.text: Option A (VPC peering), because peering propagates routes to all connected VPCs transitively, allowing any consumer VPC to reach the endpoint without additional configuration.
choices.explanation: PSC peering consumer VPCs: PSC does not peer consumer VPCs together; it only creates a private forwarding path from each consumer VPC to the service independently.

choices.text: Option A (VPC peering), because it supports overlapping CIDR ranges between the peered networks, removing IP conflict concerns entirely.
choices.explanation: VPC peering overlapping CIDRs: VPC peering explicitly requires non-overlapping IP ranges; it does not support overlapping CIDRs.

choices.text: Option B (PSC), because PSC endpoints automatically peer all consumer VPCs together, simplifying multi-VPC connectivity.
choices.explanation: VPC peering transitive routing: VPC peering is not transitive; a peered VPC cannot reach endpoints in a third VPC without additional peering agreements.

questions.explanation:
Private Service Connect exposes the Vertex AI endpoint as a private IP in each consumer VPC independently, making it IP-overlap-safe and avoiding the transitive routing constraints of peering.

**Why it works:** Each consumer VPC creates its own PSC forwarding rule with a locally assigned IP. VPCs do not need to have non-overlapping ranges with each other or with the service producer, and peering is not required between consumer VPCs.

**Why the others don't work:**
- VPC peering transitive routing: VPC peering is not transitive; a peered VPC cannot reach endpoints in a third VPC without additional peering agreements.
- VPC peering overlapping CIDRs: VPC peering explicitly requires non-overlapping IP ranges; it does not support overlapping CIDRs.
- PSC peering consumer VPCs: PSC does not peer consumer VPCs together; it only creates a private forwarding path from each consumer VPC to the service independently.

skills: 4.2.2: Deploying models to public and private endpoints.
questions.tip: Look for the two controls that together restrict both network-level access and identity-based access to a private endpoint.
questions.question:
A fintech company is deploying a credit scoring model to a Vertex AI private endpoint using Private Service Connect. The security team requires that only approved client services within specific VPCs can call the endpoint, and that only service accounts with an explicit IAM binding can invoke the model.

Which two controls BEST enforce these requirements? (Choose 2)

choices.text: Configure a PSC forwarding rule only in the approved VPCs so that the private endpoint IP is unreachable from other networks.
choices.explanation: PSC forwarding rules determine which VPCs can resolve and reach the private endpoint IP; IAM bindings ensure that even clients on approved networks must present a valid authorized identity to invoke prediction.

choices.text: Grant the `aiplatform.endpoints.predict` IAM permission only to the approved service accounts, denying prediction access to all other identities.
choices.explanation: PSC forwarding rules determine which VPCs can resolve and reach the private endpoint IP; IAM bindings ensure that even clients on approved networks must present a valid authorized identity to invoke prediction.

choices.text: Enable a public endpoint alongside the private endpoint so that approved clients can fall back to the internet path if PSC is unavailable.
choices.explanation: Public endpoint fallback: Defeats the purpose of private endpoint deployment by reintroducing an internet-accessible path.

choices.text: Set the endpoint's traffic split to 0% for the private endpoint so production traffic defaults to the public endpoint.
choices.explanation: Traffic split to 0%: Setting split to zero would route no traffic to the private endpoint, not restrict access to it.

choices.text: Use a Cloud Armor policy attached to the private endpoint to block requests from unapproved source IPs at the HTTP layer.
choices.explanation: Cloud Armor on private endpoint: Cloud Armor is not supported for Vertex AI private endpoints; it applies to external HTTP(S) load balancers fronting public endpoints.

questions.explanation:
Network isolation (PSC forwarding rules scoped to approved VPCs) and IAM-based identity control (predict permission limited to approved service accounts) together enforce both dimensions of access restriction.

**Why it works:** PSC forwarding rules determine which VPCs can resolve and reach the private endpoint IP; IAM bindings ensure that even clients on approved networks must present a valid authorized identity to invoke prediction.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Public endpoint fallback: Defeats the purpose of private endpoint deployment by reintroducing an internet-accessible path.
- Traffic split to 0%: Setting split to zero would route no traffic to the private endpoint, not restrict access to it.
- Cloud Armor on private endpoint: Cloud Armor is not supported for Vertex AI private endpoints; it applies to external HTTP(S) load balancers fronting public endpoints.

skills: 4.2.2: Deploying models to public and private endpoints.
questions.question:
The security team requires that all model prediction traffic stays within the corporate VPC and never traverses the public internet. The MLOps team plans to deploy a model to a private Agent Platform endpoint using Private Service Connect. They run the following commands.

```bash
gcloud ai endpoints create \
  --display-name=private-fraud-endpoint \
  --network=projects/123456/global/networks/ml-vpc \
  --region=us-central1

gcloud ai models deploy MODEL_ID \
  --endpoint=ENDPOINT_ID \
  --display-name=fraud-v1 \
  --machine-type=n1-standard-4 \
  --region=us-central1
```

After deployment, prediction requests from on-premises systems still fail with connection timeouts. What is MOST likely missing?

choices.text: A Private Service Connect forwarding rule has not been created in the VPC to expose the private endpoint's service attachment as an internal IP address reachable from on-premises.
choices.explanation: Agent Platform private endpoints use Private Service Connect. After creating the endpoint and deploying the model, a PSC forwarding rule must be created in the consumer VPC to expose the endpoint's service attachment as an internal IP. Without this, clients have no IP address to send requests to.

choices.text: The --network flag must specify a subnetwork rather than the VPC network for private endpoint routing to function correctly with on-premises connectivity.
choices.explanation: The --network flag correctly accepts a VPC network reference. The missing piece is the PSC forwarding rule that creates an internal IP in a subnet for clients to reach, not a change to the network flag.

choices.text: The model must be deployed with --enable-access-logging before private endpoint traffic can be established, as access logging is required to initialise the PSC connection.
choices.explanation: Access logging records request metadata for monitoring. It is not a prerequisite for establishing PSC connectivity, and disabling it would not cause connection timeouts.

choices.text: A VPC firewall rule must allow egress from the on-premises IP range to port 443 on the Agent Platform managed network before private endpoint predictions can reach the model.
choices.explanation: Firewall rules govern traffic within the VPC, but the fundamental missing piece is the PSC forwarding rule that creates a reachable internal IP. Without it, there is no destination address to which any firewall rule would apply.

questions.tip: Consider what networking object must exist in the consumer VPC before clients can address and reach a Private Service Connect endpoint.
questions.explanation:
After creating a private Agent Platform endpoint and deploying a model, the endpoint exposes a PSC service attachment. Clients in the VPC (including on-premises via VPN or Interconnect) need a PSC forwarding rule that maps the service attachment to an internal IP address in a subnet. Without this forwarding rule, there is no IP for on-premises clients to route traffic to, causing connection timeouts.

**Why it works:** Creating a PSC forwarding rule assigns an internal IP to the endpoint's service attachment, making it addressable from any client that can reach the VPC.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Subnetwork vs network: the --network flag accepts the VPC network reference correctly.
- Access logging: a monitoring feature, not a connectivity prerequisite.
- Firewall egress rule: useful but secondary; without the forwarding rule there is no destination IP for traffic.

skills: 4.2.3: Choosing appropriate hardware for serving (e.g., CPU, GPU, TPU, and edge).
questions.tip: Match the model architecture and throughput pattern to the hardware type best suited for that workload.
questions.question:
A team is deploying a large language model with 7 billion parameters to a Vertex AI endpoint. The model is transformer-based and must serve hundreds of concurrent users with throughput measured in thousands of tokens per second. Cost per token is a primary constraint.

Which hardware choice is MOST appropriate for this serving workload?

choices.text: GPU-accelerated instances (e.g., NVIDIA A100 or H100), which provide the high memory bandwidth and parallel compute required for large transformer inference at scale.
choices.explanation: NVIDIA A100/H100 GPUs have tens of gigabytes of HBM memory and thousands of CUDA cores, enabling the large matrix multiplications in transformer attention layers to run efficiently. They are supported as Vertex AI Prediction machine types for online endpoints.

choices.text: High-CPU instances (n2-highmem), which minimize cost and are sufficient for transformer models when batch sizes are kept small.
choices.explanation: High-CPU instances: CPUs lack the parallelism for transformer matrix operations; throughput would be orders of magnitude below the requirement at any practical cost.

choices.text: Edge TPU devices deployed on-premises, which reduce cloud egress costs and meet the throughput requirement.
choices.explanation: Edge TPU: Edge TPUs are low-power chips for on-device inference of small quantized models; they cannot run a 7B parameter model.

choices.text: TPU v4 pods used exclusively for offline batch inference, re-queuing real-time requests as batch jobs.
choices.explanation: TPU batch inference only: Converting real-time requests to batch jobs introduces unacceptable latency for concurrent user serving; TPU pods can serve online traffic but the framing here is incorrect.

questions.explanation:
Large transformer models require high memory bandwidth and parallel floating-point throughput that only GPU or TPU accelerators can provide; GPUs are the standard choice for flexible online serving of LLMs at scale.

**Why it works:** NVIDIA A100/H100 GPUs have tens of gigabytes of HBM memory and thousands of CUDA cores, enabling the large matrix multiplications in transformer attention layers to run efficiently. They are supported as Vertex AI Prediction machine types for online endpoints.

**Why the others don't work:**
- High-CPU instances: CPUs lack the parallelism for transformer matrix operations; throughput would be orders of magnitude below the requirement at any practical cost.
- Edge TPU: Edge TPUs are low-power chips for on-device inference of small quantized models; they cannot run a 7B parameter model.
- TPU batch inference only: Converting real-time requests to batch jobs introduces unacceptable latency for concurrent user serving; TPU pods can serve online traffic but the framing here is incorrect.

skills: 4.2.3: Choosing appropriate hardware for serving (e.g., CPU, GPU, TPU, and edge).
questions.tip: Consider the connectivity, latency, and model size constraints that determine whether a workload belongs on cloud hardware or at the edge.
questions.question:
An industrial IoT company runs quality inspection cameras on factory floors that have intermittent internet connectivity. Images must be classified within 50 ms to trigger automated reject mechanisms, and the model size is under 10 MB after quantization. The company wants to minimize cloud inference costs and tolerate offline operation.

Which hardware deployment approach is MOST suitable?

choices.text: Deploy the quantized model to Google Coral Edge TPU devices installed on the factory floor, enabling on-device inference with no cloud round-trip.
choices.explanation: Google Coral Edge TPUs are purpose-built for low-power, high-throughput edge inference of quantized models. A 10 MB quantized model fits comfortably, and all inference happens locally, satisfying both the 50 ms latency requirement and the offline operation requirement.

choices.text: Deploy the model to a Vertex AI endpoint on n2-standard CPU instances and send each image over the internet for classification.
choices.explanation: CPU cloud endpoint: A cloud round-trip alone would likely exceed 50 ms in many factory locations, and intermittent connectivity would cause inference failures.

choices.text: Deploy the model to a Vertex AI endpoint with GPU acceleration and use a message queue to buffer requests during connectivity outages.
choices.explanation: GPU cloud endpoint with message queue: Buffering in a queue violates the real-time triggering requirement; cloud round-trip latency and connectivity outages remain problematic.

choices.text: Deploy the model to Cloud Run and route camera requests through the nearest Google Cloud region to minimize latency.
choices.explanation: Cloud Run: Same network round-trip and connectivity constraints as any cloud-hosted option; cannot operate offline.

questions.explanation:
Edge TPU devices run quantized TensorFlow Lite models locally on the factory floor, achieving sub-50 ms inference with no network dependency and zero cloud inference cost.

**Why it works:** Google Coral Edge TPUs are purpose-built for low-power, high-throughput edge inference of quantized models. A 10 MB quantized model fits comfortably, and all inference happens locally, satisfying both the 50 ms latency requirement and the offline operation requirement.

**Why the others don't work:**
- CPU cloud endpoint: A cloud round-trip alone would likely exceed 50 ms in many factory locations, and intermittent connectivity would cause inference failures.
- GPU cloud endpoint with message queue: Buffering in a queue violates the real-time triggering requirement; cloud round-trip latency and connectivity outages remain problematic.

A research team is deciding between GPUs and TPUs for online serving of a 70B parameter language model that receives sustained, predictable traffic with no traffic spikes. Inference batch size is fixed at 8 and the model is implemented natively in JAX. The team prioritizes raw throughput per dollar over flexibility.

Which two characteristics of TPUs justify choosing them over GPUs for this workload? (Choose 2)

choices.text: TPUs offer significantly higher memory bandwidth per dollar for large matrix multiplications, which dominate transformer inference compute.
choices.explanation: TPU HBM delivers very high bandwidth per dollar for the matrix operations in transformer layers. The inter-chip interconnect (ICI) in TPU pods allows all-reduce operations needed for tensor parallelism to complete with minimal overhead, enabling efficient sharding of a 70B model across chips.

choices.text: TPU v4/v5 pods provide a high-bandwidth inter-chip interconnect that allows the large model to be sharded across chips with minimal communication overhead.
choices.explanation: TPU HBM delivers very high bandwidth per dollar for the matrix operations in transformer layers. The inter-chip interconnect (ICI) in TPU pods allows all-reduce operations needed for tensor parallelism to complete with minimal overhead, enabling efficient sharding of a 70B model across chips.

choices.text: TPUs support arbitrary CUDA kernels, making them compatible with any GPU-optimized inference library without code changes.
choices.explanation: Arbitrary CUDA kernels: TPUs do not execute CUDA; they use XLA compilation. GPU-optimized CUDA kernels are incompatible with TPUs.

choices.text: TPUs automatically scale to zero when traffic drops, eliminating idle compute costs for the predictable traffic pattern.
choices.explanation: Scale to zero: TPU pods on Vertex AI Prediction do not natively scale to zero; this is a characteristic of serverless CPU/GPU deployments with appropriate autoscaling config.

choices.text: TPUs use the same driver stack as NVIDIA GPUs, so JAX code can be migrated to TPU without any framework changes.
choices.explanation: Same driver stack: TPUs use Google's TPU driver and XLA, not the NVIDIA CUDA stack; JAX can target both but they are distinct backends.

questions.explanation:
For large transformer models with predictable traffic and JAX-native code, TPUs deliver superior memory bandwidth economics and efficient model sharding through their inter-chip interconnect.

**Why it works:** TPU HBM delivers very high bandwidth per dollar for the matrix operations in transformer layers. The inter-chip interconnect (ICI) in TPU pods allows all-reduce operations needed for tensor parallelism to complete with minimal overhead, enabling efficient sharding of a 70B model across chips.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Arbitrary CUDA kernels: TPUs do not execute CUDA; they use XLA compilation. GPU-optimized CUDA kernels are incompatible with TPUs.

skills: 4.2.3: Choosing appropriate hardware for serving (e.g., CPU, GPU, TPU, and edge).
