questions.question:
A solutions architect is mapping ML serving scenarios to the appropriate hardware accelerator. Each scenario has unique constraints around latency, connectivity, model size, and cost.

Match each serving scenario to the hardware type that BEST fits it.

slots.label: Scikit-learn tabular model, <1 ms latency, 100 req/s
ResNet-50 image classifier, 10 ms P99 latency, 5000 req/s
GPT-style 175B parameter model, maximum throughput, JAX-native
MobileNet quantized model on offline factory camera, <20 ms

choices.text: CPU (e.g., n2-standard): sufficient compute for small tabular models; no accelerator cost overhead.
choices.explanation: Scikit-learn tabular models have trivial compute requirements; a CPU machine like n2-standard meets the latency target without paying for an accelerator.

choices.text: GPU (e.g., NVIDIA T4 or A100): high-throughput parallel compute for deep learning inference at scale.
choices.explanation: ResNet-50 inference at 5000 requests per second requires the parallel compute of a GPU such as the T4 or A100 to meet the 10 ms P99 latency target.

choices.text: TPU v4/v5 pod: maximum memory bandwidth and inter-chip interconnect for very large model sharding.
choices.explanation: A 175B parameter JAX model needs the memory capacity and inter-chip bandwidth of a TPU v4/v5 pod, which is the design target for very large model sharding.

choices.text: Edge TPU (Coral): on-device inference for quantized models in offline or low-latency environments.
choices.explanation: An offline factory camera running a quantized MobileNet model is precisely the use case Edge TPU devices were designed for: on-device inference for quantized models with strict latency budgets.

choices.text: FPGA: custom hardware for fixed-function signal processing pipelines unrelated to ML inference.
choices.explanation: FPGAs have no role in this scenario set; they target fixed-function signal processing rather than the ML inference workloads described.

questions.explanation:
Hardware selection maps directly to model size, throughput requirements, and deployment context.

**Why it works:** Scikit-learn tabular models have trivial compute requirements; CPUs are cost-optimal. Deep learning models like ResNet-50 at high throughput require GPU parallelism. Very large models like GPT-175B need the memory capacity and inter-chip bandwidth of TPU pods. Offline edge scenarios with quantized small models are precisely the design target of Edge TPU devices.

skills: 4.2.4: Scaling the serving backend based on throughput (e.g., Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Inference and containerized serving).
questions.tip: Think about which Vertex AI autoscaling configuration knob directly controls the number of replicas available under varying load.
questions.question:
A Vertex AI online endpoint serves a recommendation model with traffic that peaks during business hours and drops to near-zero overnight. The team wants to reduce idle compute costs without completely removing serving capacity during off-peak hours.

Which autoscaling configuration achieves this goal on a Vertex AI dedicated endpoint?

choices.text: Set `minReplicaCount` to 1 and `maxReplicaCount` to 10 on the deployed model, allowing Vertex AI to scale between 1 and 10 replicas based on traffic.
choices.explanation: With `minReplicaCount=1` and `maxReplicaCount=10`, Vertex AI Prediction autoscaling keeps one replica always available (avoiding cold starts entirely) and scales out up to ten replicas as throughput increases, then scales back in as traffic falls.

choices.text: Set `minReplicaCount` to 0 and `maxReplicaCount` to 1 to enable scale-to-zero and cap costs at a single replica during peak.
choices.explanation: minReplica=0, maxReplica=1: Scale-to-zero eliminates all serving capacity overnight but also introduces cold-start latency on first request; capping max at 1 prevents handling peak load.

choices.text: Set `minReplicaCount` to 10 and `maxReplicaCount` to 10 to prevent cold-start latency at any traffic level.
choices.explanation: Fixed at 10 replicas: Eliminates autoscaling entirely; the team pays for 10 replicas at 3 AM when traffic is near-zero, directly contradicting the cost-reduction goal.

choices.text: Disable autoscaling and use a Cloud Scheduler job to manually redeploy the model each morning with increased replica counts.
choices.explanation: Cloud Scheduler redeployment: Manual scaling via redeployment is operationally fragile, introduces downtime during redeployment, and cannot respond to intra-day traffic spikes.

questions.explanation:
Setting a non-zero minimum replica count keeps at least one serving instance warm during off-peak hours while allowing scale-out to meet peak demand.

**Why it works:** With `minReplicaCount=1` and `maxReplicaCount=10`, Vertex AI Prediction autoscaling keeps one replica always available (avoiding cold starts entirely) and scales out up to ten replicas as throughput increases, then scales back in as traffic falls.

**Why the others don't work:**
- minReplica=0, maxReplica=1: Scale-to-zero eliminates all serving capacity overnight but also introduces cold-start latency on first request; capping max at 1 prevents handling peak load.
- Fixed at 10 replicas: Eliminates autoscaling entirely; the team pays for 10 replicas at 3 AM when traffic is near-zero, directly contradicting the cost-reduction goal.
- Cloud Scheduler redeployment: Manual scaling via redeployment is operationally fragile, introduces downtime during redeployment, and cannot respond to intra-day traffic spikes.

skills: 4.2.4: Scaling the serving backend based on throughput (e.g., Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Inference and containerized serving).
questions.tip: When containerized serving on GKE uses a custom metric like GPU utilization rather than CPU, the autoscaler must be configured to target that specific signal.
questions.question:
An ML team containerizes a TensorFlow Serving image and deploys it to Google Kubernetes Engine. At 70% GPU utilization the latency P99 breaches SLA; at below 30% the deployment is over-provisioned. The team wants to autoscale pods automatically based on GPU utilization using a Kubernetes-native mechanism.

Which configuration BEST enables GPU-utilization-based autoscaling for this deployment?

choices.text: Configure a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler targeting a custom metric exported from GPU utilization (e.g., via DCGM Exporter and Cloud Monitoring adapter) with a target average value of 50%.
choices.explanation: DCGM (Data Center GPU Manager) Exporter exposes per-GPU utilization metrics to Prometheus; the Cloud Monitoring or Prometheus adapter makes these available to HPA as custom metrics. Setting a target of 50% GPU utilization keeps the workload in the efficient range and scales pods before the 70% SLA-breach threshold is reached.

choices.text: Configure the HPA to target CPU utilization at 50%, as GPU load is always proportional to CPU load for TensorFlow Serving workloads.
choices.explanation: CPU utilization proxy: For GPU-bound inference, CPU utilization is not reliably proportional to GPU load; scaling on CPU would either over- or under-provision GPU capacity.

choices.text: Enable GKE Autopilot and rely on its built-in node provisioner to automatically allocate GPU nodes based on inference queue depth.
choices.explanation: GKE Autopilot queue depth: Autopilot scales nodes, not pods based on GPU utilization; it does not natively expose GPU utilization as an HPA target without additional instrumentation.

choices.text: Use a Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) to increase GPU memory allocation when utilization is high, replacing the need for horizontal scaling.
choices.explanation: Vertical Pod Autoscaler: VPA adjusts resource requests per pod (CPU/memory), not GPU allocation; it does not scale the number of pods and cannot increase GPU memory beyond the physical GPU limit.

questions.explanation:
Kubernetes HPA supports custom and external metrics, allowing GPU utilization exported via DCGM Exporter to drive pod scaling decisions precisely.

**Why it works:** DCGM (Data Center GPU Manager) Exporter exposes per-GPU utilization metrics to Prometheus; the Cloud Monitoring or Prometheus adapter makes these available to HPA as custom metrics. Setting a target of 50% GPU utilization keeps the workload in the efficient range and scales pods before the 70% SLA-breach threshold is reached.

**Why the others don't work:**
- CPU utilization proxy: For GPU-bound inference, CPU utilization is not reliably proportional to GPU load; scaling on CPU would either over- or under-provision GPU capacity.
- GKE Autopilot queue depth: Autopilot scales nodes, not pods based on GPU utilization; it does not natively expose GPU utilization as an HPA target without additional instrumentation.
- Vertical Pod Autoscaler: VPA adjusts resource requests per pod (CPU/memory), not GPU allocation; it does not scale the number of pods and cannot increase GPU memory beyond the physical GPU limit.

skills: 4.2.4: Scaling the serving backend based on throughput (e.g., Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Inference and containerized serving).
questions.tip: Think about the two architectural levers that each reduce per-request cost or increase throughput independently.
questions.question:
A media company's content moderation model receives 50,000 requests per minute with highly variable inter-arrival rates. The current Vertex AI dedicated endpoint is frequently over-provisioned, wasting GPU capacity during lulls. The ML engineering team wants to improve cost efficiency and throughput without migrating away from Vertex AI managed serving.

Which two changes MOST directly improve throughput efficiency on the Vertex AI endpoint? (Choose 2)

choices.text: Enable request batching on the serving container to group concurrent requests into larger batches, increasing GPU utilization per forward pass.
choices.explanation: Batching combines multiple concurrent requests into a single forward pass, increasing GPU occupancy without additional replicas. Autoscaling adjusts replica count to match observed throughput, eliminating the cost of idle replicas during lulls.

choices.text: Configure autoscaling with a target-utilization threshold so that replica count scales down during traffic lulls and scales out during spikes.
choices.explanation: Batching combines multiple concurrent requests into a single forward pass, increasing GPU occupancy without additional replicas. Autoscaling adjusts replica count to match observed throughput, eliminating the cost of idle replicas during lulls.

choices.text: Increase `maxReplicaCount` to a very large number without configuring a scale-in policy, ensuring replicas never terminate during brief lulls.
choices.explanation: Very large maxReplica without scale-in: Prevents cost reduction during lulls; replicas persist even when unnecessary, which is the root problem the team is trying to solve.

choices.text: Switch the endpoint from dedicated resources to shared resources to reduce per-minute compute cost regardless of traffic pattern.
choices.explanation: Shared resources: Shared endpoints do not provide dedicated GPU capacity; for 50k RPM the lack of guaranteed throughput would likely cause latency SLA breaches.

choices.text: Move inference to a batch prediction job triggered every minute to amortize GPU startup costs across the full request volume.
choices.explanation: Batch prediction job: Batch prediction is designed for asynchronous offline workloads; triggering it every minute introduces 30-60 second latency windows, inappropriate for content moderation.

questions.explanation:
Request batching and autoscaling address the two root causes of inefficiency: low GPU utilization per request and replica count mismatched to actual traffic.

**Why it works:** Batching combines multiple concurrent requests into a single forward pass, increasing GPU occupancy without additional replicas. Autoscaling adjusts replica count to match observed throughput, eliminating the cost of idle replicas during lulls.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Very large maxReplica without scale-in: Prevents cost reduction during lulls; replicas persist even when unnecessary, which is the root problem the team is trying to solve.
- Shared resources: Shared endpoints do not provide dedicated GPU capacity; for 50k RPM the lack of guaranteed throughput would likely cause latency SLA breaches.
- Batch prediction job: Batch prediction is designed for asynchronous offline workloads; triggering it every minute introduces 30-60 second latency windows, inappropriate for content moderation.

questions.tip: Container images must be published before they can be pulled by GKE; monitoring must be configured before the autoscaler can read its target metric.
questions.question:
An ML engineer is setting up a containerized model serving deployment on GKE with GPU-based autoscaling driven by a custom throughput metric. The engineer needs to follow the correct provisioning sequence to avoid dependency failures.

Arrange the following steps in the correct order.

choices.text: Build the TensorFlow Serving Docker image and push it to Artifact Registry.
choices.explanation: Each step has a hard dependency on the previous one.

choices.text: Deploy the serving container to GKE as a Deployment with GPU resource requests, referencing the Artifact Registry image.
choices.explanation: A GKE Deployment referencing a non-existent image will fail to start.

choices.text: Install DCGM Exporter on GPU nodes and configure the Cloud Monitoring Prometheus adapter to expose GPU utilization as a custom metric.
choices.explanation: DCGM Exporter can only report GPU utilization from pods that are already running.

choices.text: Create an HPA resource targeting the custom GPU utilization metric with a defined target average value.
choices.explanation: The HPA creation will fail or malfunction if the custom metric it targets does not yet exist in the metrics adapter.

choices.text: Run a load test and verify that pod count scales out as GPU utilization crosses the HPA target threshold.
choices.explanation: Load testing is the final validation that all components interact correctly.

questions.explanation:
The container image must exist before GKE can pull it; the Deployment must run before DCGM can export metrics from its GPU; the metric must be available before the HPA can reference it; load testing validates the complete autoscaling chain.

**Why it works:** Each step has a hard dependency on the previous one. A GKE Deployment referencing a non-existent image will fail to start. DCGM Exporter can only report GPU utilization from pods that are already running. The HPA creation will fail or malfunction if the custom metric it targets does not yet exist in the metrics adapter. Load testing is the final validation that all components interact correctly.

skills: 4.2.5: Tuning ML models for training and serving in production.
questions.tip: Think about which optimization technique directly reduces the memory footprint and arithmetic precision of a model without retraining from scratch.
questions.question:
A computer vision team has a production ResNet-50 model served on a GPU endpoint. The model achieves 95% accuracy but the inference latency is 80 ms P99, exceeding the 50 ms SLA. The team wants to reduce latency with MINIMAL impact to model accuracy and without retraining the model from the beginning.

Which optimization technique should the team apply FIRST?

choices.text: Apply post-training quantization to convert FP32 weights to INT8, then export the model with TensorRT to generate an optimized inference engine.
choices.explanation: INT8 quantization reduces weight precision from 32 bits to 8 bits, halving or quartering memory bandwidth consumption and enabling Tensor Core acceleration. TensorRT fuses layers, applies kernel auto-tuning, and generates a GPU-optimized execution plan, collectively achieving significant latency reduction.

choices.text: Retrain the model from scratch using FP16 mixed-precision training and a smaller learning rate to produce a natively smaller model.
choices.explanation: Retraining with FP16: Requires a full training run, which is expensive and time-consuming; it addresses training efficiency, not post-hoc inference optimization.

choices.text: Apply structured pruning to remove 50% of the model's filters and then fine-tune on the full training set for 100 epochs to recover accuracy.
choices.explanation: Structured pruning with fine-tuning: Pruning can reduce latency, but requiring 100 epochs of fine-tuning is expensive and is not the minimal-effort first step.

choices.text: Replace ResNet-50 with a MobileNetV3 architecture trained from scratch, accepting a 5% accuracy drop to meet the latency target.
choices.explanation: Replacing with MobileNetV3: Choosing a completely different architecture requires training from scratch and explicitly accepts an accuracy drop, violating the minimal accuracy impact constraint.

questions.explanation:
Post-training INT8 quantization followed by TensorRT compilation is the lowest-effort path to latency reduction because it requires no retraining and typically reduces inference time by 2-4x on NVIDIA GPUs.

**Why it works:** INT8 quantization reduces weight precision from 32 bits to 8 bits, halving or quartering memory bandwidth consumption and enabling Tensor Core acceleration. TensorRT fuses layers, applies kernel auto-tuning, and generates a GPU-optimized execution plan, collectively achieving significant latency reduction.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Retraining with FP16: Requires a full training run, which is expensive and time-consuming; it addresses training efficiency, not post-hoc inference optimization.
- Structured pruning with fine-tuning: Pruning can reduce latency, but requiring 100 epochs of fine-tuning is expensive and is not the minimal-effort first step.
- Replacing with MobileNetV3: Choosing a completely different architecture requires training from scratch and explicitly accepts an accuracy drop, violating the minimal accuracy impact constraint.

skills: 4.2.5: Tuning ML models for training and serving in production.
questions.tip: Consider where repeated identical computations or lookups can be intercepted and cached before they reach the model.
questions.question:
A production NLP model classifies support tickets into routing categories. Monitoring reveals that 40% of inference requests are for identical ticket text submitted by automation scripts that retry on failure. Each request incurs a full GPU forward pass costing 30 ms. The P50 latency target is 10 ms, but retraining or model compression has already been exhausted.

Which serving-layer optimization MOST directly addresses this specific traffic pattern?

choices.text: Implement a semantic cache layer using Cloud Memorystore for Redis, keyed on a hash of the input text, to return cached predictions for repeated identical inputs without invoking the model.
choices.explanation: With 40% of requests being exact duplicates, a Redis-based cache keyed on a deterministic hash of the input text will achieve a high hit rate. Cache hits bypass the model completely, reducing effective P50 latency well below the 30 ms forward-pass time and toward the 10 ms target.

choices.text: Increase the number of GPU replicas behind the endpoint to reduce queuing delay for the repeated requests.
choices.explanation: More GPU replicas: Additional replicas reduce queuing latency but still execute a full 30 ms forward pass for every request, including duplicates; this does not approach the 10 ms P50 target.

choices.text: Enable request batching on the endpoint to group repeated requests into larger batches, reducing per-request GPU overhead.
choices.explanation: Request batching: Batching amortizes GPU overhead across requests but still processes all requests including duplicates; it reduces cost per request but not the latency of individual duplicate requests.

choices.text: Apply knowledge distillation to train a smaller student model that can classify repeat requests faster than the current teacher model.
choices.explanation: Knowledge distillation: Distillation produces a faster model but requires a training pipeline and the result still processes every request, including duplicates; the unique pattern here is exact repetition, which caching exploits more directly.

questions.explanation:
A prediction cache keyed on input hash intercepts repeat requests before they reach the model, returning stored results in sub-millisecond time and entirely eliminating the GPU cost for those requests.

**Why it works:** With 40% of requests being exact duplicates, a Redis-based cache keyed on a deterministic hash of the input text will achieve a high hit rate. Cache hits bypass the model completely, reducing effective P50 latency well below the 30 ms forward-pass time and toward the 10 ms target.

**Why the others don't work:**
- More GPU replicas: Additional replicas reduce queuing latency but still execute a full 30 ms forward pass for every request, including duplicates; this does not approach the 10 ms P50 target.
- Request batching: Batching amortizes GPU overhead across requests but still processes all requests including duplicates; it reduces cost per request but not the latency of individual duplicate requests.
- Knowledge distillation: Distillation produces a faster model but requires a training pipeline and the result still processes every request, including duplicates; the unique pattern here is exact repetition, which caching exploits more directly.

skills: 4.2.5: Tuning ML models for training and serving in production.
questions.tip: Think about the two optimization techniques that reduce model size or arithmetic cost at the weight level without requiring labeled data for retraining.
questions.question:
A team is preparing a BERT-base model for production serving on NVIDIA T4 GPUs. The model currently runs at FP32 precision and has 110 million parameters. Latency must be halved and the model size must fit within 150 MB. The team has no labeled training data available for fine-tuning after optimization.

Which two optimization techniques can the team apply without requiring labeled training data? (Choose 2)

choices.text: Apply dynamic quantization to convert linear layer weights from FP32 to INT8 at load time, reducing model size and accelerating CPU and GPU inference.
choices.explanation: Dynamic quantization converts weights at load time using only the weight statistics already embedded in the model file; no calibration dataset is needed. ONNX Runtime applies graph-level optimizations (op fusion, constant folding, layout optimization) to the exported model graph without any training.

choices.text: Export the model to ONNX format and run ONNX Runtime with graph optimizations enabled, fusing operations and eliminating redundant nodes.
choices.explanation: Dynamic quantization converts weights at load time using only the weight statistics already embedded in the model file; no calibration dataset is needed. ONNX Runtime applies graph-level optimizations (op fusion, constant folding, layout optimization) to the exported model graph without any training.

choices.text: Apply knowledge distillation using the FP32 BERT model as a teacher to train a smaller 6-layer student BERT model on the original labeled training set.
choices.explanation: Knowledge distillation: Requires running the teacher model to generate soft labels on a dataset, then training the student; labeled data or at least a large unlabeled dataset is needed for effective distillation.

choices.text: Perform structured pruning on the attention heads and fine-tune for 5 epochs on the task-specific labeled dataset to recover accuracy.
choices.explanation: Structured pruning with fine-tuning: Fine-tuning after pruning explicitly requires a labeled task-specific dataset, which the team does not have.

choices.text: Retrain BERT from scratch with a vocabulary reduced by 50% to decrease embedding table size and speed up tokenization.
choices.explanation: Retraining from scratch: Requires the full pretraining corpus and labeled downstream data; this is the most data-intensive option and contradicts the constraint.

questions.explanation:
Dynamic quantization and ONNX Runtime graph optimization both improve serving efficiency without requiring labeled data or any retraining.

**Why it works:** Dynamic quantization converts weights at load time using only the weight statistics already embedded in the model file; no calibration dataset is needed. ONNX Runtime applies graph-level optimizations (op fusion, constant folding, layout optimization) to the exported model graph without any training.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Knowledge distillation: Requires running the teacher model to generate soft labels on a dataset, then training the student; labeled data or at least a large unlabeled dataset is needed for effective distillation.
- Structured pruning with fine-tuning: Fine-tuning after pruning explicitly requires a labeled task-specific dataset, which the team does not have.
- Retraining from scratch: Requires the full pretraining corpus and labeled downstream data; this is the most data-intensive option and contradicts the constraint.

skills: 4.2.5: Tuning ML models for training and serving in production.
questions.question:
The team needs to reduce the serving latency of a PyTorch classification model deployed on CPU-only Agent Platform endpoints. The model is currently 350 MB and takes 120 ms per request. A team member applies the following optimisation.

```python
import torch

model.eval()

model_quantized = torch.quantization.quantize_dynamic(
    model,
    {torch.nn.Linear},
    dtype=torch.qint8
)

torch.save(model_quantized.state_dict(), 'model_quantized.pt')
print(f'Original: {get_size(model):.1f} MB')
print(f'Quantized: {get_size(model_quantized):.1f} MB')
```

What does this code accomplish and what is a key trade-off?

choices.text: It applies dynamic quantisation to convert Linear layer weights from float32 to int8, reducing model size and CPU inference time at the potential cost of a small accuracy reduction.
choices.explanation: quantize_dynamic replaces float32 weights in the specified layer types with int8 representations. This reduces model size by ~4x for those layers and speeds up CPU matrix multiplication, with a typically small accuracy trade-off.

choices.text: It converts the model to a static computation graph using TorchScript, reducing Python interpreter overhead and enabling deployment without a Python runtime.
choices.explanation: torch.quantization.quantize_dynamic performs weight quantisation, not TorchScript compilation. TorchScript conversion uses torch.jit.script() or torch.jit.trace().

choices.text: It prunes all Linear layer weights below a threshold of qint8, removing near-zero parameters and reducing the effective model size without any accuracy trade-off.
choices.explanation: Quantisation maps floating-point values to a discrete integer range - it does not prune or remove weights. Pruning is a separate technique that sets weights to zero and requires sparse execution support.

choices.text: It applies quantisation-aware training by inserting fake quantisation nodes into the computation graph, requiring a brief fine-tuning pass to recover accuracy.
choices.explanation: quantize_dynamic is post-training dynamic quantisation - it runs on an already-trained model with no fine-tuning required. Quantisation-aware training uses torch.quantization.prepare_qat() and requires a training loop.

questions.tip: Consider what 'dynamic' quantisation means compared to static quantisation and quantisation-aware training.
questions.explanation:
Dynamic quantisation converts specified layer weights (here, `torch.nn.Linear`) from float32 to int8 at model save time, with activations quantised dynamically at inference time. This reduces the model size ~4x for those layers and speeds up CPU inference, but may introduce a small accuracy drop due to the reduced numeric precision.

**Why it works:** int8 matrix multiplication is significantly faster on CPUs than float32, and reduced model size lowers memory bandwidth requirements.

**Why the others don't work:**
- TorchScript: quantize_dynamic is for weight precision reduction, not compilation.
- Pruning: removes weights; quantisation remaps their values to a coarser range.
- Quantisation-aware training: requires a training loop; quantize_dynamic is entirely post-training.

skills: 5.1.1: Validating data and models within pipelines.
questions.question: Your data engineering team is building a TFX pipeline for a fraud detection model. During a recent incident the pipeline trained on a batch where a critical numeric feature had a much different value range than the training baseline, producing poor predictions. You want the pipeline to automatically detect such anomalies and halt before training begins. Which TFX component should you add?

choices.text: ExampleValidator
choices.explanation: ExampleValidator takes the output of StatisticsGen and SchemaGen as inputs, then flags anomalies such as out-of-range values, unexpected feature distributions, and missing features. When anomalies are detected, downstream components can be gated to prevent training on bad data.

choices.text: SchemaGen
choices.explanation: SchemaGen: Infers the schema from training data but does not perform validation or anomaly detection on new batches.

choices.text: StatisticsGen
choices.explanation: StatisticsGen: Computes descriptive statistics about a dataset but does not compare them to a baseline or flag anomalies.

choices.text: Evaluator
choices.explanation: Evaluator: Assesses model performance against a threshold after training, not data quality before training.

questions.tip: Among the TFX data validation components, only one compares a new batch's statistics to a baseline schema and surfaces anomalies before training.
questions.explanation:
ExampleValidator is the correct component for detecting anomalies in input data by comparing computed statistics against an expected schema.

**Why it works:** ExampleValidator takes the output of StatisticsGen and SchemaGen as inputs, then flags anomalies such as out-of-range values, unexpected feature distributions, and missing features. When anomalies are detected, downstream components can be gated to prevent training on bad data.

**Why the others don't work:**
- SchemaGen: Infers the schema from training data but does not perform validation or anomaly detection on new batches.

questions.question:
The team is building a TFX pipeline and wants to detect schema anomalies in each new batch of training data before the training step runs. A team member adds the following components.

```python
from tfx.components import (
    CsvExampleGen, StatisticsGen, SchemaGen, ExampleValidator
)

example_gen = CsvExampleGen(input_base=data_root)
statistics_gen = StatisticsGen(examples=example_gen.outputs['examples'])
schema_gen = SchemaGen(statistics=statistics_gen.outputs['statistics'])
validator = ExampleValidator(
    statistics=statistics_gen.outputs['statistics'],
    schema=schema_gen.outputs['schema']
)
```

On the second pipeline run, the validator raises no anomalies even though a new feature was added to the data that was absent from the original schema. What is MOST likely causing this?

choices.text: SchemaGen regenerates a new schema from the current run's statistics on every execution, so the new feature is included in the schema before ExampleValidator checks against it, suppressing the anomaly.
choices.explanation: SchemaGen derives a schema from the current batch's statistics. If SchemaGen runs on each pipeline execution, the generated schema always reflects the current data - meaning ExampleValidator finds no mismatch because the schema already includes the new feature.

choices.text: ExampleValidator only detects anomalies in the training split and silently ignores the evaluation split, so new features that appear only in training are never flagged.
choices.explanation: ExampleValidator can validate both splits. The issue is that SchemaGen generates a fresh schema from the current data, not that evaluation splits are excluded.

choices.text: The CsvExampleGen component caches its output from the first run and does not re-read the updated CSV files, so ExampleValidator still sees the original feature set.
choices.explanation: TFX component caching can reuse previous outputs, but ExampleValidator's anomaly detection would not be silenced by CsvExampleGen caching if a fresh schema was also generated. The root cause is SchemaGen regenerating the schema from current statistics.

choices.text: ExampleValidator requires a minimum of three pipeline runs to establish a statistical baseline before it begins flagging schema deviations from the original schema.
choices.explanation: ExampleValidator compares current statistics against a provided schema immediately on each run. There is no minimum run count before anomaly detection activates.

questions.tip: Consider what schema ExampleValidator is validating against - is it fixed from the first run or regenerated each time?
questions.explanation:
The pipeline regenerates the schema via SchemaGen on every run, so by the time ExampleValidator runs, the schema already includes the new feature. To detect deviations from an approved baseline, the schema should be curated and frozen (e.g., stored in a schema file and loaded via ImportSchemaGen) rather than regenerated from the current data. ExampleValidator then validates incoming statistics against the stable, human-approved schema.

**Why it works:** A fixed baseline schema captures the approved feature set. Any new or missing feature in incoming data produces an anomaly.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Split filtering: ExampleValidator validates all splits; split behaviour is not the cause.
- CsvExampleGen caching: even with cached data, a regenerated schema would match it.
- Three-run baseline: ExampleValidator has no such warm-up requirement.

Which of the following code snippets correctly defines a KFP v2 pipeline that chains an `ingest` component into a `train` component using the output of `ingest` as input to `train`?

choices.explanation: In KFP v2, each component task exposes its declared outputs via the `.outputs` dict, keyed by the output parameter name. Passing `ingest_task.outputs['dataset']` to `train` creates an explicit data dependency, which the compiler uses to construct the pipeline DAG and wire the artifact URI automatically at runtime.

choices.text:
```python
@pipeline(name='my-pipeline')
def my_pipeline():
    ingest_task = ingest()
    train_task = train(dataset=ingest_task.output)
    train_task.after(ingest_task)
```
choices.explanation: Option using `.artifact('dataset')`: `.artifact()` is not a method in the KFP v2 DSL; this would raise an `AttributeError` at pipeline compilation time.

choices.text:
```python
@pipeline(name='my-pipeline')
def my_pipeline():
    ingest_task = ingest()
    train_task = train(dataset=ingest_task.outputs)
    pipeline.connect(ingest_task, train_task)
```
choices.explanation: Option using `.outputs` (dict) and `pipeline.connect()`: `pipeline.connect()` is not a valid KFP v2 API. Passing the entire `.outputs` dict without a key would also not type-check correctly.

Option using `.output` and `.after()`: `.output` (singular) is used only when a component has a single unnamed output. Using `.after()` adds an ordering constraint but does not pass the artifact value, so `train` would not receive the dataset.

questions.question:
The team is defining an Agent Platform Pipeline using the Kubeflow Pipelines v2 SDK. They write the following pipeline definition.

```python
from kfp.v2 import dsl

@dsl.pipeline(name='training-pipeline')
def training_pipeline(data_path: str, epochs: int = 10):
    preprocess_task = preprocess_data(data_path=data_path)
    train_task = train_model(
        processed_data=preprocess_task.outputs['processed_data'],
        epochs=epochs
    )
    evaluate_task = evaluate_model(
        model=train_task.outputs['model'],
        test_data=preprocess_task.outputs['test_data']
    )
    with dsl.Condition(evaluate_task.outputs['accuracy'] > 0.85):
        register_task = register_model(
            model=train_task.outputs['model']
        )
```

What does `dsl.Condition` accomplish in this pipeline definition?

choices.text: It creates a conditional branch so that register_model only executes if the accuracy output from evaluate_model exceeds 0.85, preventing low-quality models from being registered automatically.
choices.explanation: dsl.Condition in KFP v2 defines a conditional execution gate. Steps inside the with block are only scheduled and executed if the specified condition evaluates to True at pipeline runtime.

choices.text: It runs the register_model step in parallel with evaluate_model and only forwards the model artifact if accuracy exceeds 0.85, merging the two outputs at the end.
choices.explanation: dsl.Condition gates sequential execution - it does not create parallel branches. register_model depends on evaluate_model's output and runs after evaluation, not in parallel.

choices.text: It retries the entire pipeline from the preprocess step if accuracy falls below 0.85, feeding new data into the pipeline until the threshold is reached.
choices.explanation: dsl.Condition controls whether a step executes, not whether the pipeline retries from the beginning. Retry behaviour is configured per-task using task.set_retry().

choices.text: It validates that the accuracy output is a float at compile time and raises a TypeError if the evaluate_model component returns a non-numeric value.
choices.explanation: dsl.Condition is evaluated at pipeline runtime against the actual output values, not at compile time. Type validation of component outputs is handled separately by the KFP SDK's type system.

questions.tip: Consider when and under what circumstances the steps inside a dsl.Condition block are executed.
questions.explanation:
`dsl.Condition` defines a conditional execution gate in KFP v2. At runtime, after `evaluate_model` completes, the pipeline evaluates whether `accuracy > 0.85`. If True, `register_model` is scheduled and executed. If False, the block is skipped entirely. This prevents automatically registering models that do not meet a quality threshold.

**Why it works:** The conditional gate makes model registration a quality-gated step, implementing a promotion policy directly in the pipeline DAG.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Parallel branch: dsl.Condition is sequential gating, not parallelism.
- Pipeline retry: retry is per-task, not per-condition block.
- Compile-time validation: conditions are evaluated at runtime against actual outputs.

questions.question: Your team trained a regression model with a TFX pipeline that uses the Transform component to normalize numeric features and compute vocabulary encodings. After deploying the model behind a separate Python preprocessing service that the team wrote by hand, online prediction quality is much worse than offline evaluation suggested. You want to fix the training-serving skew while minimizing duplicated preprocessing code. What should you do?

choices.text: Replace the custom preprocessing service with the SavedModel preprocessing graph that TFX Transform exported, and serve it together with the trained model on Vertex AI Prediction.
choices.explanation: TFX Transform writes the preprocessing logic to a SavedModel that can be attached to the trained model. Reusing this graph at serving time guarantees that features are computed identically to training, eliminating the source of skew.

choices.text: Tighten the Evaluator component thresholds so that any model whose offline metrics regress is blocked from promotion.
choices.explanation: Evaluator gates model promotion on quality metrics. It does not change how features are computed at serving time, so the skew between the two preprocessing implementations would persist.

choices.text: Add an ExampleValidator stage to the serving pipeline so that any feature distribution that diverges from the training schema is flagged before prediction.
choices.explanation: ExampleValidator detects schema and distribution anomalies, which is useful for monitoring, but it does not reconcile the two different preprocessing implementations that produced the divergent values in the first place.

choices.text: Re-export the trained model to a different Cloud Storage path and update the serving service to load the model artifact from the new location.
choices.explanation: The skew described is in feature values, not model weights, so loading the same model from a different path changes nothing about the preprocessing mismatch.

questions.tip: TFX Transform exports a SavedModel that contains the preprocessing graph; reusing it at serving time is what eliminates skew.
questions.explanation:
The root cause is that two different preprocessing implementations are running, one in TFX Transform during training and one in the custom Python service at serving time. Vocabulary ordering, numeric precision, or rounding differences between them produce skew.

**Why it works:** TFX Transform produces a SavedModel preprocessing graph that captures the exact transformations applied during training. Serving this graph alongside the trained model (or attaching it to the model itself) guarantees identical feature computation in production.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Tightening Evaluator: only gates promotion based on offline metrics; it does not unify preprocessing.
- Adding ExampleValidator at serving: detects anomalies but does not eliminate the dual implementation.
- Re-exporting to a new path: the model weights are not the issue; the preprocessing logic is.
